messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, February 28, 2013 4:07:17 PM UTC-5, Seth Flaxman wrote:
> Thanks Bob and Ben. I am still trying to get this working in the
> soft-k-means case. (I like the idea of lkj_cov and will try that soon.
> Any good examples?)
>
> I tried the attached (two ways are listed there), but I'm running into
> the symmetry problem Ben identified:
>
> Exception: Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function
> soft_k_means2_model_namespace::write_csv(d): Sigma is not symmetric.
> Sigma[0,5] is 4.8734081952257217e-317, but Sigma[5,0] element is
> 0.220718
> Diagnostic information:
> Dynamic exception type: std::domain_error
> std::exception::what: Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function
> soft_k_means2_model_namespace::write_csv(d): Sigma is not symmetric.
> Sigma[0,5] is 4.8734081952257217e-317, but Sigma[5,0] element is
> 0.220718

Sigma is KxK rather than MxM, so Bob's / my code should have been

> >> for(k in 1:K) {
> >>    Sigma[k,k] <- square(sigma[k]);
> >>    for(n in (k+1):K) {
> >>      Sigma[k,n] <- sigma[k] * sigma[n] * Omega[k,n];
> >>      Sigma[n,k] <- Sigma[k,n];
> >>    }
> >> }

In which case, it is a bug that it actually managed to get through the adaptation phase with the wrong code.

Ben

On Feb 27, 2013, at 6:18 PM, atzap wrote:

> Thanks for the quick reply Andrew G. and sorry again for the dense rambling post.
>
> Please download the workspace linked above (https://dl.dropbox.com/u/7489119/Workspace3.RData) and then open up the Rscript3.txt file.  You will see that the output in the object fit.stan looks like it has converged but the heidel.diag and geweke.diag tests suggest otherwise for some of the parameters (e.g. ran's and taualpha).  More importantly, the following quote:
> > > despite what neff, Rhat, and visual inspection of the chain traces
> may be more relevant for the JAGS result.  Again, please see the jagsfit8 object in the linked workspace.  The within-chain diagnostics from coda suggest that some parameters in some of the chains haven't converged, and this is especially true when we compare the result to STAN and the lmer function.
>
> Again, thanks for STAN!  Its performance is continuing to impress when compared to the other tools that are out there.
> Andrew
>
>
>
> On Wednesday, February 27, 2013 5:39:35 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Hi, Andrew T.  I'm glad that Stan is helpful.  Just quickly:  the R-hat we use now is a split R-hat, which includes within as well as between-chain information.  So I don't think it should happen that the chains aren't really converging despite what neff, Rhat, and visual inspection of the chain traces say.  If this _is_ happening, I'd like to understand what's going on.  So if you could send the example of the results that weren't converging despite Rhat etc., please do so and I can take a look.  Thanks.
> > AG
> >
> > On Feb 27, 2013, at 5:36 PM, atzap wrote:
> >
> > > >
> > > > A fair point!  I've plotted out the rans’s and alpha’s and they don't look particularly correlated.  However, running for longer and using the within-chain diagnostics (Geweke; Heidelberg and Welch) shows that the chains aren't really converging despite what neff, Rhat, and visual inspection of the chain traces say...  I’ve also tried making the level of alpha with only 1 observation an additive inverse of the other two.  The result is that JAGS continues to go to a different place in parameter space than STAN, i.e. beta's are non-overlapping zero while alpha's are in STAN.   Though, the model is still not converging even after very long runs (millions of iterations).
> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: correlated topic model code
messages.body_plain:
The code you've attached uses a global covariance structure.
You could also fit covariance cluster-by cluster, so that
instead of

   cov_matrix[D] Sigma; // covariance matrix

you'd have a covariance matrix for each cluster,

   cov_matrix[D] Sigma[K]; // covariance matrix for cluster

The other thing to do is try to get a simpler model
working first.   Does the output look OK with simpler
soft K-means?

You also have a much stronger prior on the means (normal(0,1))
than on the variances ([half] cauchy(0,5)).  That should be OK for
this data, which looks fairly well behaved.

- Bob

> This is a limitation of the between-chain variance vs. within-chain variance approach to convergence diagnostics (and effective sample size calculations). For your longer runs, can you check whether some of the purely within-chain convergence diagnostics in the coda package indicate lack of convergence for the chains individually?

So I'm getting a funny feeling about these within-chain convergence diagnostics in coda.  If I run the two that I've been using on the schools example, they suggest that the individual chains haven't converged!

# run schools example
fit.stan <- stan(model_code = schools_code, data = schools_dat,iter = 10000, warmup = 8000, thin = 10, chains = 4)

# calculate p-values (if you believe in such things) associated with Z-scores from Geweke on each chain

round(2*pnorm(-abs(sapply(geweke.diag(fit.stan2), function(x){x$z}))), 3)

# calculate Heidel on each chain
heidel.diag(fit.stan2)

Clearly, this is nonsense, isn't it?  So does that mean we shouldn't be overly concerned about these specific diagnostics, especially the half-width mean test?  In which case, we return to my original issue, which is that assuming the models have converged, JAGS throws up different parameter estimates than STAN...  Sorry if I'm flogging a dead horse.

The idea is to compare the neighborhoods to where the chains converge with the stepsize varying but stepsize*treedepth held constant.  NUTS should ensure that stepsize*treedepth is constant provided you don't hit the maximum tree depth, so I would make sure to raise the maximum tree depth for these studies.

If there are weird geometric issues then the chains with smaller stepsizes will be different than the chains with the larger stepsizes.  If they are consistent than there's no obvious issue on the HMC/NUTS side.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dump Data Format
messages.body_plain:
JSON's a good idea for an I/O format.

The motivation for the S-like structure is
that it was easy for us to generate the output and
it's what we already had data for in all the models
we wanted to test in JAGS.

At least it was supposed to be easy, but R's dump
output is rather idiosyncratic (the format varies
by content, so the output format for array { 1, 2, 3 }
is different than that for { 1, 2, 4}.

Presumably JSON could deal with ragged arrays, which
would also be very useful.

- Bob

messages.subject: JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
There's a boost lib that parses JSON into a
DOM-like property tree:

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/doc/html/property_tree.html

We'd just need to implement our data interface on top of
a property tree the same way we have done for reading
from files and reading from the R environment.

I'm less clear on JSON output -- I don't see anything
to write JSON-formatted data, though it's bound to
be a lot easier than parsing if we need to write it
ourselves.  The output needs to come in the form of
headers and then lines of data, and will hopefully be
streamable.

We might literally be able to set a compiled Stan
model up to work as a pipe taking JSON-formatted
data as standard input and producing JSON-formatted
data as standard output with control given by the
command-line options of the compiled Stan model.   With
that, a fully-functional, basic Python interface should
be really simple.

- Bob

The primary problem is this line:

PRED[n] <- A*Y1[n] + dot_product(MUS,X[n]) + dot_product(B[n+1].*Q, Z[n]);

B is a (N+1)xK matrix and Q is 1xK. But B[n+1] is the n+1th element of B. Perhaps you meant row(B, n+1) ?

Similar, Z[n] is the nth element of Z rather than the nth row. Perhaps you meant transpose(row(Z,n)) ?

Ben

gets a single type that's declared?  Otherwise, our matrix

is a vector or vice-versa.  It will work if they're both
matrices of the same dimension.

- Bob

messages.subject: Possible regression in stan 1.1.*
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I just thought I should let you know that the attached model works without a problem on rstan 1.0.3 installed through R 2.15.3 on Windows 7 (64-bit version), but not with rstan 1.1.1. By "not working" I mean the model does not compile when using set_cppo("debug"), and does compile with set_cppo("fast") but when run makes Windows freeze up by using up all available RAM on 64-bit R (except with an extremely small dataset) or crashing under 32-bit R. If there are any more details I can or should provide (e.g. messages when crashing) please let me know.

Guy

PS. A "#340" error forced me to change the extension of the stan model file.

response and few covariates (1-3).

best

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] question about the transformed parameter block
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave,

The additional benefit of using the transformed parameter block is the ability to use constraints on the variables. The constraints are checked once per leapfrog step, which adds a little computational overhead, but can help trap modeling errors early.

If you want a more detailed explanation, there is a chapter in the manual on Program Blocks. The overview subsection discusses how frequently each of the blocks are executed.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: PyStan
messages.body_plain:
I've used python to run Stan for a recently-submitted paper. Since I was just trying to get my experiments run, after a few minutes of establishing that it'd be a nontrivial amount of work to write a python interface directly, I instead wrote an interface to use RStan through python (via the rpy2 bridge): https://gist.github.com/dougalsutherland/5093571.

This worked okay for me and may be useful to others, though it feels a little silly and certainly complicates the toolchain to add R into the mix. All this code lets you do is compile models with stan_model() and then extract() the results of sampling() from it, though that's just because that's all I needed; it shouldn't be hard to wrap any of the other R functions. It also currently caches compiled models by pickling the rpy2 object; it might be preferable to save and load models in R-land, but as someone who's never used R before I was having trouble getting that to work and opted for the zero-effort solution instead.

I looked briefly into the possibility of writing an interface to the sampler model, but didn't want to go through the work of writing a stan::io::var_context implementation and so on. Also, Python's C++ interoperability isn't great; AFAIK your options are
write C wrappers to your C++ API and then call them through ctypes, Cython, etc
use Boost::Python, which I've attempted to learn and found to be an enormous chore due mainly to the crazy build system they insist on using
use Cython's C++ support, which isn't especially well-documented and I had troubles with when I last attempted it a year ago
use the Python C APIs manually, which is presumably not that hard but I've never tried.
I'd be happy to work on a real, direct Python interface to Stan. I wonder if the best approach might not be, though, to first make an easy-to-use C wrapper for compiled Stan models. This would make Stan easier to wrap for Python and other languages that have good C interaction but nothing like RCpp with such good C++ interaction.

- Dougal

>
> Andrew

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, March 6, 2013 5:04:48 PM UTC-5, Irene Zeng wrote:
> Dear Mailing users,
> I am starting to use Rstan only recently. I have run 4 chains sampling in my laptop, after 4 days, it finish the first chain of sampling, but it showed up a error message " cannot allocate vector of size 8kb". I still want to have the results of the first chain, is there a way to get the first chain samples ? How would I know how much memeory I need if I need to run 4 chains ?

There is an option for stan() called sample_file that can be passed a character string to write the samples to a file. In addition, it is possible to call stan() in parallel using any of the parallel frameworks that R supports. The main problem with memory in your model is that you define mu as a transformed parameter that has length 78400! Even if you wrote the samples to a disk, you could easily crash R when you loaded them into RAM. I personally would define mu as a local vector in the model section so that its samples are used but not stored. In addition, it is wasteful to embark on a 4 day run without optimizing your code. The main areas where your code would go faster are using matrix algebra rather than scalar algebra, using the vectorized forms of the distributions rather than manually looping over all the observations, and using bernoulli_logit() instead of bernoulli(inv_logit(...)).

Ben

messages.subject: Stan 1.2.0 & RStan 1.2.0 released
messages.body_plain:
Stan 1.2.0 and RStan 1.2.0 are now available for download.
See:

     http://mc-stan.org/

Here are the highlights.

1.  Full Mass Matrix Estimation during Warmup

Yuanjun Gao, a first-year grad student here at Columbia (!),
built a regularized mass-matrix estimator.   This helps
for posteriors with high correlation among parameters
and varying scales.  We're still testing this ourselves, so
the estimation procedure may change in the future.

It's not the default option.  The major reason is the matrix
operations required are expensive, raising the algorithm
cost to O(K * M * N^2 + log(M) N^3), where K is the average
number of leapfrog steps, M is the number of iterations, and
N is the number of parameters.

Yuanjun did a great job with the Cholesky factorizations
and implemented this about as efficiently as is possible.
(His homework for Andrew's class was also the inspiration
for the Gaussian process models in the manual.)

It's integrated with NUTS.

2.  Cumulative Distribution Functions

The practical upshot is that Stan supports more truncated
distributions, and hence more truncated and censored data models.

Michael Betancourt did the heavy lifting here, which involved a crazy
amount of "special function" derivative calculations and implementations.
Everyone knows that the derivative of a distribution function with respect
to the variate is the density.  But what about the partials with respect to the other
parameters?  We'll be documenting all of the functions and derivatives
in the manual.

Daniel Lee generalized the entire density and distribution function
testing framework to generate code for tests.  We're doing much more
extensive tests of the vectorizations and derivatives.  Also, Daniel
implemented efficient vectorized derivatives for many more of the density
functions.

3.  Model Log Probability and Derivatives in R

Jiqiang Guo, who's at the helm of RStan, wrote code to allow users
to access the log probability function in a Stan model and its gradients
directly.  The functions are parameterized with the unconstrained
parameterization of a Stan model with support on all of R^N.  He
also exposed the model functions to convert back and forth between
the constrained and unconstrained parameterizations for initialization
and interpretation of the samples.

David Blei suggested that if we added this feature, people
could do interesting things in R with it, such as optimization.
Let us know if you find it helpful.

4.  Print Posterior Summary Statistics from Command Line

Daniel Lee wrote a program to print a summary of one or more chains
from the command line, mirroring the print() command of RStan.

5.  Bug Fixes

We also fixed a bad memory leak in multivariate operations that
was introduced in the last release when we optimized the matrix
operations for derivative calculations.  We also fixed the Windows
issue with conservative matrix resizing which caused multivariate
models to crash under Windows at optimization levels above 0.

There's also been a lot going on in various branches that haven't
been merged into the trunk yet, so stay tuned.

- Stan Development Team

P.S.  Here are the release notes.

v1.2.0 (6 March 2012)
======================================================================

Enhancements
----------------------------------
* full mass matrix estimation during warmup
* expose model log_prob and gradient functions in RStan for use
   in other packages (such as optimizers)
* command-line program to display output from multiple chains
   with parameter-by-parameter mean, se, sd, quantiles, and R-hat
* probability function speed improvements with vectorization
* created Stan contributed repositories for user-contributed
   and experimental features (first entry is an emacs mode)
* modified makefiles so targets are the same under Windows,
   Linux, and Mac

New Functions
----------------------------------
* most of the cumulative distribution functions (see the documentation
   index for the full list of supported functions)
* added monitor() function in RStan

Bug Fixes
----------------------------------
* disabled Boost asserts in parser to quiet R's warnings
* enabled prints in generated quantities block
* various documentation patches
* fixed memory leak in matrix operations leading to leaks in
   multivariate probability function use
* wrapped call to gradient log prob to catch unexpected exceptions
* fixed matrix resize issue on Windows that caused models to fail
   at optimization levels above 0
* fixed bug in print preventing hyphens or grave accents from
   priting
* fixed issue preventing matrix rows from being assigned on the
   left side of an assignment statement
* clearer error messages on matrix and other function arguments

messages.body_plain:
This sounds like a great idea. Using json as data interchange format makes it easier for developers to interface to stan, without having to study and implement the data-dump format. One can easily write wrappers for all kinds of third party languages, unix pipes, RPC protocols, etc. Plus, by building on a standardized format like json, you get a lot of stuff for free, e.g. basic validation, a schema language, or storing I/O directly in a json database like mongo. It will make the software accessible to a much greater community.

> There's a boost lib that parses JSON into a
> DOM-like property tree:
>
>   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/doc/html/property_tree.html
>
> We'd just need to implement our data interface on top of
> a property tree the same way we have done for reading
> from files and reading from the R environment.
>
> I'm less clear on JSON output -- I don't see anything
> to write JSON-formatted data, though it's bound to
> be a lot easier than parsing if we need to write it
> ourselves.  The output needs to come in the form of
> headers and then lines of data, and will hopefully be
> streamable.
>
> We might literally be able to set a compiled Stan
> model up to work as a pipe taking JSON-formatted
> data as standard input and producing JSON-formatted
> data as standard output with control given by the
> command-line options of the compiled Stan model.   With
> that, a fully-functional, basic Python interface should
> be really simple.
>
> - Bob

python wrapper as a unix-pipe-oriented CLI wrapper, which would be
pretty inefficient, compared to a python wrapper that uses a compiled
model as/via a DLL? Maybe I've missed the point.

Dan

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for all  your suggestions for optimizing codes.I did not expect it run so long and do not want to interrupt it in the middle :d) It looks like the model section can be similar as the bug language.
I have used multi_normal() function for the sampling , but I had a error message as below, so I change to univariate normal for the trial. Do you know why I will get such message although I just copy the code for multinormal function ? thanks! Irene
g~multi_normal(mn,invprec);
 ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
no matches for function name="multi_normal_log"
    arg 0 type=real[1]
    arg 1 type=real[1]
    arg 2 type=matrix
unknown distribution=multi_normal
Parser expecting: "}"
> print(fit)
Stan model 'protein_code' does not contain samples.
> plot(fit)
Stan model 'protein_code' does not contain samples.

On Thursday, March 7, 2013 11:34:18 AM UTC+13, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, March 6, 2013 5:04:48 PM UTC-5, Irene Zeng wrote:
> > Dear Mailing users,
> > I am starting to use Rstan only recently. I have run 4 chains sampling in my laptop, after 4 days, it finish the first chain of sampling, but it showed up a error message " cannot allocate vector of size 8kb". I still want to have the results of the first chain, is there a way to get the first chain samples ? How would I know how much memeory I need if I need to run 4 chains ?
>
> There is an option for stan() called sample_file that can be passed a character string to write the samples to a file. In addition, it is possible to call stan() in parallel using any of the parallel frameworks that R supports. The main problem with memory in your model is that you define mu as a transformed parameter that has length 78400! Even if you wrote the samples to a disk, you could easily crash R when you loaded them into RAM. I personally would define mu as a local vector in the model section so that its samples are used but not stored. In addition, it is wasteful to embark on a 4 day run without optimizing your code. The main areas where your code would go faster are using matrix algebra rather than scalar algebra, using the vectorized forms of the distributions rather than manually looping over all the observations, and using bernoulli_logit() instead of bernoulli(inv_logit(...)).
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Advice on Hierarchical Model
messages.body_plain:
The segfault you saw in the previous message should never
happen.  If it does, it's either a bug in our code (most likely)
or a corruption of memory in the hardware (less likely).

So I'm glad you're not seeing it in 1.2.0.

The main places segfaults can creep in is if we don't properly
allocate an array or test its bounds during access, or if we
don't properly allocate a parameter, transformed parameter,
or local variable in a model.

As to the model itself, the basic idea looks OK at first
glance.  And fitting simpler models first is absolutely the
right way to go.  But this looks wrong:

  for(j in 1:N_agencies)
      a_type[[type[j],1] ~ normal(0, 100);

You almost certainly want to sample a_type in a loop over the types,
like this:

   for (t in 1:N_types)
       a_type[t,1] ~ normal(0,100);

As is, you are implicitly specifying the prior as a product
of normal(0,100) distributions, one for each agency with the
given type.  This is legal syntax in Stan, but BUGS would flag
it as illegal.

The same goes for the rest of the time series.  So you want
to break this out into two loops --- one for a_type, and one
for a_agency.

I suggest (1) applying a transform to the normals (aka the
Matt trick, as described in the manual), and (2)
vectorizing.  (1) should speed convergence, and (2) should
speed up each iteration.

Also, if you can provide sensible initial values it'll help
for regressions with lots of parameters.  Or try initializing
to 0 to see if that helps get at least one chain toward its
destination.

- Bob

multi_normal requires a vector for the variate and location
arguments (vector).  You're giving it arrays (real[1]).

So you must have something declared as

    real g[N];

which should be declared as

    vector[N] g;

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
We'd implement JSON I/O completely independently of Python.

That'd certainly make it easier to call in the unix pipe style
from Python or other languages.  But I think the original poster's
suggestion was that it'd just be easier to write the necessary
Stan input files and parse Stan output files if they were in
a standard format like JSON instead of the quirky dump format that
R inherited from S.

There are advantages to a simple pipe-like interface --- it
requires far less maintenance and documentation.  The RStan
interface wraps a dynamic lib (which is a DLL on Windows) at
the memory level rather than going through files.  But that
means whenever the command-line interface changes (for instance
we add a new sampler type as we just did for 1.2), the Python
program has to change.

Python looks like it'll let us do a deeper API-style integration
if we wanted, rather than just implementing the command.  So
we might wrap up our current samplers (implemented as iterators)
in Python iterators.

I think most users would probably like the command, though, implemented
either as a pipe to one or more external processes or through memory/dynamic
linking.

- Bob

Wrapping C/C++ code from python can be done in many ways. This is a good overview of the pros and cons of each approach http://scipy-lectures.github.com/advanced/interfacing_with_c/interfacing_with_c.html

On Tue, Mar 5, 2013 at 12:05 PM, Dougal Sutherland <dou...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I've used python to run Stan for a recently-submitted paper. Since I was just trying to get my experiments run, after a few minutes of establishing that it'd be a nontrivial amount of work to write a python interface directly, I instead wrote an interface to use RStan through python (via the rpy2 bridge): https://gist.github.com/dougalsutherland/5093571.
>
> This worked okay for me and may be useful to others, though it feels a little silly and certainly complicates the toolchain to add R into the mix. All this code lets you do is compile models with stan_model() and then extract() the results of sampling() from it, though that's just because that's all I needed; it shouldn't be hard to wrap any of the other R functions. It also currently caches compiled models by pickling the rpy2 object; it might be preferable to save and load models in R-land, but as someone who's never used R before I was having trouble getting that to work and opted for the zero-effort solution instead.
>
>
> I looked briefly into the possibility of writing an interface to the sampler model, but didn't want to go through the work of writing a stan::io::var_context implementation and so on. Also, Python's C++ interoperability isn't great; AFAIK your options are
> write C wrappers to your C++ API and then call them through ctypes, Cython, etc
> use Boost::Python, which I've attempted to learn and found to be an enormous chore due mainly to the crazy build system they insist on using
> use Cython's C++ support, which isn't especially well-documented and I had troubles with when I last attempted it a year ago
> use the Python C APIs manually, which is presumably not that hard but I've never tried.
> I'd be happy to work on a real, direct Python interface to Stan. I wonder if the best approach might not be, though, to first make an easy-to-use C wrapper for compiled Stan models. This would make Stan easier to wrap for Python and other languages that have good C interaction but nothing like RCpp with such good C++ interaction.
>
> - Dougal
>
>
> On Monday, March 4, 2013 11:53:35 AM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Stan is written in C++ and can be run from the command line and from R. We’d like for Python users to be able to run Stan as well. If anyone is interested in doing this, please let us know and we’d be happy to work with you on it!
> >
> > Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Stan 1.2.0 & RStan 1.2.0 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan devs,
Where can I find more detail about the mass matrix estimation routine?  Also, I was wondering if the Riemannian approach in future releases will allow users to define their own metric or if the default will be Fisher-Rao?

Thanks,
akhil

On Wednesday, March 6, 2013 6:40:48 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Stan 1.2.0 and RStan 1.2.0 are now available for download.
> See:
>
>      http://mc-stan.org/
>
> Here are the highlights.
>
>
> 1.  Full Mass Matrix Estimation during Warmup
>
> Yuanjun Gao, a first-year grad student here at Columbia (!),
> built a regularized mass-matrix estimator.   This helps
> for posteriors with high correlation among parameters
> and varying scales.  We're still testing this ourselves, so
> the estimation procedure may change in the future.
>
> It's not the default option.  The major reason is the matrix
> operations required are expensive, raising the algorithm
> cost to O(K * M * N^2 + log(M) N^3), where K is the average
> number of leapfrog steps, M is the number of iterations, and
> N is the number of parameters.
>
> Yuanjun did a great job with the Cholesky factorizations
> and implemented this about as efficiently as is possible.
> (His homework for Andrew's class was also the inspiration
> for the Gaussian process models in the manual.)
>
> It's integrated with NUTS.
>
>
> 2.  Cumulative Distribution Functions
>
> The practical upshot is that Stan supports more truncated
> distributions, and hence more truncated and censored data models.
>
> Michael Betancourt did the heavy lifting here, which involved a crazy
> amount of "special function" derivative calculations and implementations.
> Everyone knows that the derivative of a distribution function with respect
> to the variate is the density.  But what about the partials with respect to the other
> parameters?  We'll be documenting all of the functions and derivatives
> in the manual.
>
> Daniel Lee generalized the entire density and distribution function
> testing framework to generate code for tests.  We're doing much more
> extensive tests of the vectorizations and derivatives.  Also, Daniel
> implemented efficient vectorized derivatives for many more of the density
> functions.
>
>
> 3.  Model Log Probability and Derivatives in R
>
> Jiqiang Guo, who's at the helm of RStan, wrote code to allow users
> to access the log probability function in a Stan model and its gradients
> directly.  The functions are parameterized with the unconstrained
> parameterization of a Stan model with support on all of R^N.  He
> also exposed the model functions to convert back and forth between
> the constrained and unconstrained parameterizations for initialization
> and interpretation of the samples.
>
> David Blei suggested that if we added this feature, people
> could do interesting things in R with it, such as optimization.
> Let us know if you find it helpful.
>
>
> 4.  Print Posterior Summary Statistics from Command Line
>
> Daniel Lee wrote a program to print a summary of one or more chains
> from the command line, mirroring the print() command of RStan.
>
>
> 5.  Bug Fixes
>
> We also fixed a bad memory leak in multivariate operations that
> was introduced in the last release when we optimized the matrix
> operations for derivative calculations.  We also fixed the Windows
> issue with conservative matrix resizing which caused multivariate
> models to crash under Windows at optimization levels above 0.
>
>
> There's also been a lot going on in various branches that haven't
> been merged into the trunk yet, so stay tuned.
>
> - Stan Development Team
>
>
> P.S.  Here are the release notes.
>
>
> v1.2.0 (6 March 2012)
> ======================================================================
>
> Enhancements
> ----------------------------------
> * full mass matrix estimation during warmup
> * expose model log_prob and gradient functions in RStan for use
>    in other packages (such as optimizers)
> * command-line program to display output from multiple chains
>    with parameter-by-parameter mean, se, sd, quantiles, and R-hat
> * probability function speed improvements with vectorization
> * created Stan contributed repositories for user-contributed
>    and experimental features (first entry is an emacs mode)
> * modified makefiles so targets are the same under Windows,
>    Linux, and Mac
>
> New Functions
> ----------------------------------
> * most of the cumulative distribution functions (see the documentation
>    index for the full list of supported functions)
> * added monitor() function in RStan
>
> Bug Fixes
> ----------------------------------
> * disabled Boost asserts in parser to quiet R's warnings
> * enabled prints in generated quantities block
> * various documentation patches
> * fixed memory leak in matrix operations leading to leaks in
>    multivariate probability function use
> * wrapped call to gradient log prob to catch unexpected exceptions
> * fixed matrix resize issue on Windows that caused models to fail
>    at optimization levels above 0
> * fixed bug in print preventing hyphens or grave accents from
>    priting
> * fixed issue preventing matrix rows from being assigned on the
>    left side of an assignment statement
> * clearer error messages on matrix and other function arguments

messages.body_plain:
The mass matrix estimation routine is Yuanjun's.

It regularizes toward the diagonal matrix of variances and
toward the identity matrix.  Like the diagonal estimation that's the default,
it works during warmup by (roughly) using the last half of the
warmup to estimate (it actually does this as it goes along, so
the mass matrix gets updated during warmup).  Yuanjun's writing
up a paper that'll have all the details.

We'll start with Michael Betancourt's SoftAbs metric and maybe
the diagonal approximate SoftAbs, too:

   http://arxiv.org/pdf/1212.4693.pdf

We're working on refactoring the HMC code to make it all
much more configurable at the C++ level.

The metric will definitely be plug-and-play at the C++ level.
Any suggestions on how to make it user configurable through
the Stan command and RStan?  My inclination would be to name a class
that is used in a template somewhere and instantiated in the code.

We also need to work on user-defined functions of other kinds, so
maybe we can do both of these at the same time.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraining parameters in stationary models
messages.body_plain:
On 3/7/13 1:49 PM, Carlos wrote:> Hi all!

 >
 > I was wondering if it is possible to constrain the parameters when there
 > are several restrictions that should be met.
 > For example, in a stationary autoregressive process of order 2,
 >
 >   Y(t) =phi1*Y(t-1) + phi2*(t-2)
 >
 > we want that,
 >
 >   phi1 + phi2 < 1
 >   phi1 - phi2< 1
 >   abs(phi2) < 1

Funny you should bring that up.  I've had it on our
to-do list for a while.  When I asked Andrew, he suggested
it would be a bad idea to do this because the data should
constrain the solution to be stationary if the process
actually is stationary and you don't want to constrain it to
a stationary solution if it's not.

I'm more interested in what you can do with Stan, not whether
it's a good idea statistically :-)

The stationary constraints above are captured by:

   real <lower=-1,upper=1> phi2;
   real <upper=(1 - fabs(phi2))> phi1;

The constraint on phi2 is the one you pointed out.  The
second pair of equations can be rewritten as:

    phi1 < 1 - phi2
    phi1 < 1 + phi2

and we know

   1 - abs(phi2) = min(1 - phi2, 1 + phi2).

 > More generally, if we have an autoregressive process of order P,
 > is it possible to restrict the roots of the p-th order
 > polynomial to lie outside the unit circle?

But if you really want to do this, one approach is to
parameterize in terms of the roots and then define the
coefficients as transformed parameters.

But if you want priors on the coefficients
instead of the roots, you need to add the log absolute determinant
of the Jacobian to lp__.

Both of these calcs gets messy at higher orders.

Or maybe priors on the roots will suggest different models?
What Andrew calls the Pinocchio Principle.

- Bob

Well, I think that Andrew has a very good point  here :D But... at least my experience is that when you have highly autocorrelated processes (let's say, an AR(1) model with phi=0.9), if I put a non-constrained prior, and I allow the support to be R, even if in general the chain of the parameter is inside (-1,1), sometimes there are outliers such that abs(phi)>1. If we want to focus on means, ok, that is not a problem. But if we want to compute impulse response functions, and want to extract the quantiles by simulation, sometimes the paths explode, and I think that might be difficult to extract good conclusions about them. Also, I was thinking in more complicated models, like a Vector Autorregression. Even if the data is stationary, it is quite difficult to extract draws from a conjugate prior (multivariate normal distribution and an Inverse Wishart) such that the draw leads to a stationary path. I think that Gary Koop has a paper on that (he finds the rejection rate to be around 90% or more in a standard Gibbs Sampler, such that he discards any draw that does not lead to a stationary process).   But this is just given my (little) experience :D

But if you want priors on the coefficients instead of the roots, you need to add the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian to lp__. Both of these calcs gets messy at higher orders.

Mmmm, I will probably have to think of this. If there are one-to-one mappings from the roots to the coefficients, should not be any problem, but I am not sure about that. In any case, as you said, I guess that the calcs will get terribly difficult...

Or maybe priors on the roots will suggest different models?

messages.body_plain:
Incidentally, this is another reason for Yuanjun to write up his paper.  Once it's written up, others can read it and maybe come up with improvements!

On Mar 7, 2013, at 1:20 PM, akhil wrote:

> Hi Stan devs,
> Where can I find more detail about the mass matrix estimation routine?  Also, I was wondering if the Riemannian approach in future releases will allow users to define their own metric or if the default will be Fisher-Rao?
>
> Thanks,
> akhil
>
>
> On Wednesday, March 6, 2013 6:40:48 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Stan 1.2.0 and RStan 1.2.0 are now available for download.
> > See:
> >
> >      http://mc-stan.org/
> >
> > Here are the highlights.
> >
> >
> > 1.  Full Mass Matrix Estimation during Warmup
> >
> > Yuanjun Gao, a first-year grad student here at Columbia (!),
> > built a regularized mass-matrix estimator.   This helps
> > for posteriors with high correlation among parameters
> > and varying scales.  We're still testing this ourselves, so
> > the estimation procedure may change in the future.
> >
> > It's not the default option.  The major reason is the matrix
> > operations required are expensive, raising the algorithm
> > cost to O(K * M * N^2 + log(M) N^3), where K is the average
> > number of leapfrog steps, M is the number of iterations, and
> > N is the number of parameters.
> >
> > Yuanjun did a great job with the Cholesky factorizations
> > and implemented this about as efficiently as is possible.
> > (His homework for Andrew's class was also the inspiration
> > for the Gaussian process models in the manual.)
> >
> > It's integrated with NUTS.
> >
> >
> > 2.  Cumulative Distribution Functions
> >
> > The practical upshot is that Stan supports more truncated
> > distributions, and hence more truncated and censored data models.
> >
> > Michael Betancourt did the heavy lifting here, which involved a crazy
> > amount of "special function" derivative calculations and implementations.
> > Everyone knows that the derivative of a distribution function with respect
> > to the variate is the density.  But what about the partials with respect to the other
> > parameters?  We'll be documenting all of the functions and derivatives
> > in the manual.
> >
> > Daniel Lee generalized the entire density and distribution function
> > testing framework to generate code for tests.  We're doing much more
> > extensive tests of the vectorizations and derivatives.  Also, Daniel
> > implemented efficient vectorized derivatives for many more of the density
> > functions.
> >
> >
> > 3.  Model Log Probability and Derivatives in R
> >
> > Jiqiang Guo, who's at the helm of RStan, wrote code to allow users
> > to access the log probability function in a Stan model and its gradients
> > directly.  The functions are parameterized with the unconstrained
> > parameterization of a Stan model with support on all of R^N.  He
> > also exposed the model functions to convert back and forth between
> > the constrained and unconstrained parameterizations for initialization
> > and interpretation of the samples.
> >
> > David Blei suggested that if we added this feature, people
> > could do interesting things in R with it, such as optimization.
> > Let us know if you find it helpful.
> >
> >
> > 4.  Print Posterior Summary Statistics from Command Line
> >
> > Daniel Lee wrote a program to print a summary of one or more chains
> > from the command line, mirroring the print() command of RStan.
> >
> >
> > 5.  Bug Fixes

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraining parameters in stationary models
messages.body_plain:
One way to implement this in Stan would be to define a new datatype for a vector which is in the AR stationarity and invertibility region. The function ARtransPars in the R package dlm maps between the reals and AR parameters using the method defined the following paper,

Jones, 1987. Randomly choosing parameters from the stationarity and invertibility region of autoregressive-moving average models. Applied Statistics, 36.

On Thu, Mar 7, 2013 at 3:19 PM, Carlos <car...@montesgaldon.com> wrote:

> > Funny you should bring that up.  I've had it on our
> > to-do list for a while.  When I asked Andrew, he suggested
> > it would be a bad idea to do this because the data should
> > constrain the solution to be stationary if the process
> > actually is stationary and you don't want to constrain it to
> > a stationary solution if it's not.
>
> Well, I think that Andrew has a very good point  here :D But... at least my experience is that when you have highly autocorrelated processes (let's say, an AR(1) model with phi=0.9), if I put a non-constrained prior, and I allow the support to be R, even if in general the chain of the parameter is inside (-1,1), sometimes there are outliers such that abs(phi)>1. If we want to focus on means, ok, that is not a problem. But if we want to compute impulse response functions, and want to extract the quantiles by simulation, sometimes the paths explode, and I think that might be difficult to extract good conclusions about them. Also, I was thinking in more complicated models, like a Vector Autorregression. Even if the data is stationary, it is quite difficult to extract draws from a conjugate prior (multivariate normal distribution and an Inverse Wishart) such that the draw leads to a stationary path. I think that Gary Koop has a paper on that (he finds the rejection rate to be around 90% or more in a standard Gibbs Sampler, such that he discards any draw that does not lead to a stationary process).   But this is just given my (little) experience :D
>
> > The stationary constraints above are captured by:
> >
> >    real <lower=-1,upper=1> phi2;
> >    real <upper=(1 - fabs(phi2))> phi1;
> >
> > The constraint on phi2 is the one you pointed out.  The
> > second pair of equations can be rewritten as:
> >
> >     phi1 < 1 - phi2
> >     phi1 < 1 + phi2
> >
> > and we know
> >
> >    1 - abs(phi2) = min(1 - phi2, 1 + phi2).
>
> I didn't know that we can use parameters in the bounds!! This is very good news!.
>
> >  But if you really want to do this, one approach is to parameterize in terms of the roots and then define the coefficients as transformed parameters. But if you want priors on the coefficients instead of the roots, you need to add the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian to lp__. Both of these calcs gets messy at higher orders.
>
> Mmmm, I will probably have to think of this. If there are one-to-one mappings from the roots to the coefficients, should not be any problem, but I am not sure about that. In any case, as you said, I guess that the calcs will get terribly difficult...
>
> Or maybe priors on the roots will suggest different models?
> What Andrew calls the Pinocchio Principle.

> On Thursday, March 7, 2013 2:19:55 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > On 3/7/13 1:49 PM, Carlos wrote:> Hi all!
> >  >
> >  > I was wondering if it is possible to constrain the parameters when there
> >  > are several restrictions that should be met.
> >  > For example, in a stationary autoregressive process of order 2,
> >  >
> >  >   Y(t) =phi1*Y(t-1) + phi2*(t-2)
> >  >
> >  > we want that,
> >  >
> >  >   phi1 + phi2 < 1
> >  >   phi1 - phi2< 1
> >  >   abs(phi2) < 1
> >
> > Funny you should bring that up.  I've had it on our
> > to-do list for a while.  When I asked Andrew, he suggested
> > it would be a bad idea to do this because the data should
> > constrain the solution to be stationary if the process
> > actually is stationary and you don't want to constrain it to
> > a stationary solution if it's not.
> >
> > I'm more interested in what you can do with Stan, not whether
> > it's a good idea statistically :-)
> >
> > The stationary constraints above are captured by:
> >
> >    real <lower=-1,upper=1> phi2;
> >    real <upper=(1 - fabs(phi2))> phi1;
> >
> > The constraint on phi2 is the one you pointed out.  The
> > second pair of equations can be rewritten as:
> >
> >     phi1 < 1 - phi2
> >     phi1 < 1 + phi2
> >
> > and we know
> >
> >    1 - abs(phi2) = min(1 - phi2, 1 + phi2).
> >
> >  > More generally, if we have an autoregressive process of order P,
> >  > is it possible to restrict the roots of the p-th order
> >  > polynomial to lie outside the unit circle?
> >
> > But if you really want to do this, one approach is to
> > parameterize in terms of the roots and then define the
> > coefficients as transformed parameters.
> >
> > But if you want priors on the coefficients
> > instead of the roots, you need to add the log absolute determinant
> > of the Jacobian to lp__.
> >
> > Both of these calcs gets messy at higher orders.
> >
> > Or maybe priors on the roots will suggest different models?
> > What Andrew calls the Pinocchio Principle.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >

Yes! This should work! I think that even the recursion might be implemented in a standard STAN code, even without creating the data type (although it would be much more convenient, of course!)

On Thursday, March 7, 2013 6:27:55 PM UTC-5, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
> One way to implement this in Stan would be to define a new datatype for a vector which is in the AR stationarity and invertibility region. The function ARtransPars in the R package dlm maps between the reals and AR parameters using the method defined the following paper,
>
> Jones, 1987. Randomly choosing parameters from the stationarity and invertibility region of autoregressive-moving average models. Applied Statistics, 36.
>
> On Thu, Mar 7, 2013 at 3:19 PM, Carlos <car...@montesgaldon.com> wrote:
> > > Funny you should bring that up.  I've had it on our
> > > to-do list for a while.  When I asked Andrew, he suggested
> > > it would be a bad idea to do this because the data should
> > > constrain the solution to be stationary if the process
> > > actually is stationary and you don't want to constrain it to
> > > a stationary solution if it's not.
> >
> > Well, I think that Andrew has a very good point  here :D But... at least my experience is that when you have highly autocorrelated processes (let's say, an AR(1) model with phi=0.9), if I put a non-constrained prior, and I allow the support to be R, even if in general the chain of the parameter is inside (-1,1), sometimes there are outliers such that abs(phi)>1. If we want to focus on means, ok, that is not a problem. But if we want to compute impulse response functions, and want to extract the quantiles by simulation, sometimes the paths explode, and I think that might be difficult to extract good conclusions about them. Also, I was thinking in more complicated models, like a Vector Autorregression. Even if the data is stationary, it is quite difficult to extract draws from a conjugate prior (multivariate normal distribution and an Inverse Wishart) such that the draw leads to a stationary path. I think that Gary Koop has a paper on that (he finds the rejection rate to be around 90% or more in a standard Gibbs Sampler, such that he discards any draw that does not lead to a stationary process).   But this is just given my (little) experience :D
> >
> > > The stationary constraints above are captured by:
> > >
> > >    real <lower=-1,upper=1> phi2;
> > >    real <upper=(1 - fabs(phi2))> phi1;
> > >
> > > The constraint on phi2 is the one you pointed out.  The
> > > second pair of equations can be rewritten as:
> > >
> > >     phi1 < 1 - phi2
> > >     phi1 < 1 + phi2
> > >
> > > and we know
> > >
> > >    1 - abs(phi2) = min(1 - phi2, 1 + phi2).
> >
> > I didn't know that we can use parameters in the bounds!! This is very good news!.
> >
> > >  But if you really want to do this, one approach is to parameterize in terms of the roots and then define the coefficients as transformed parameters. But if you want priors on the coefficients instead of the roots, you need to add the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian to lp__. Both of these calcs gets messy at higher orders.
> >
> > Mmmm, I will probably have to think of this. If there are one-to-one mappings from the roots to the coefficients, should not be any problem, but I am not sure about that. In any case, as you said, I guess that the calcs will get terribly difficult...
> >
> > Or maybe priors on the roots will suggest different models?
> > What Andrew calls the Pinocchio Principle.
> > On Thursday, March 7, 2013 2:19:55 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > On 3/7/13 1:49 PM, Carlos wrote:> Hi all!
> > >  >
> > >  > I was wondering if it is possible to constrain the parameters when there
> > >  > are several restrictions that should be met.
> > >  > For example, in a stationary autoregressive process of order 2,
> > >  >
> > >  >   Y(t) =phi1*Y(t-1) + phi2*(t-2)
> > >  >
> > >  > we want that,
> > >  >
> > >  >   phi1 + phi2 < 1
> > >  >   phi1 - phi2< 1
> > >  >   abs(phi2) < 1
> > >
> > > Funny you should bring that up.  I've had it on our
> > > to-do list for a while.  When I asked Andrew, he suggested
> > > it would be a bad idea to do this because the data should
> > > constrain the solution to be stationary if the process
> > > actually is stationary and you don't want to constrain it to
> > > a stationary solution if it's not.
> > >
> > > I'm more interested in what you can do with Stan, not whether
> > > it's a good idea statistically :-)
> > >
> > > The stationary constraints above are captured by:
> > >
> > >    real <lower=-1,upper=1> phi2;
> > >    real <upper=(1 - fabs(phi2))> phi1;
> > >
> > > The constraint on phi2 is the one you pointed out.  The
> > > second pair of equations can be rewritten as:
> > >
> > >     phi1 < 1 - phi2
> > >     phi1 < 1 + phi2
> > >
> > > and we know
> > >
> > >    1 - abs(phi2) = min(1 - phi2, 1 + phi2).
> > >
> > >  > More generally, if we have an autoregressive process of order P,
> > >  > is it possible to restrict the roots of the p-th order
> > >  > polynomial to lie outside the unit circle?
> > >
> > > But if you really want to do this, one approach is to
> > > parameterize in terms of the roots and then define the
> > > coefficients as transformed parameters.
> > >
> > > But if you want priors on the coefficients
> > > instead of the roots, you need to add the log absolute determinant
> > > of the Jacobian to lp__.
> > >
> > > Both of these calcs gets messy at higher orders.
> > >
> > > Or maybe priors on the roots will suggest different models?
> > > What Andrew calls the Pinocchio Principle.
> > >
> > > - Bob

On 3/8/13 10:02 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Friday, March 8, 2013 4:23:17 AM UTC-5, Irene wrote:
>
>     thanks, you are right. I change the declaration for g and mn as vector[] , the message gone. Now I also want to sample
>     the row vector of the matrix U[200,3] from multi_normal distribution, I have tried several version. this is the last
>     one,
>     but not work..Irene
>
>
> I don't think multi_normal is defined for row vectors. Only column vectors and matrices.

Correct.  You can find a convenient list of all the
signatures for all the functions supported by Stan in
the index.

So what you need to do is apply a transpose. So if x
is the column vector, instead of writing "x ~ multi_normal(...)"
write "x' ~ multi_normal(...)".  Same for the location vector,
which also has to be a vector.

We'll probably generalize the multivariate normal when
we get around to vectorizing it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Scope of "model" block variables and access to them subsequently
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Scope of "model" block variables and access to them subsequently
messages.body_plain:
Answers inline.

On 3/9/13 5:11 PM, Rudolf Cardinal wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I've just come across Stan and am very impressed; thanks to all those who have developed it!
>
> I'm trying to use it for reinforcement learning models in which some information is stored locally (in the "model"
> block) and used to calculate things on a trial-by-trial, cumulative basis. Stan seems potentially ideal for this, given
> that you can do imperative coding within the "model" block.
>

> The Stan manual (v1.2.0) says (under "Variable scope") that "*The variables declared in each block have scope over all
> subsequent statements.* Thus a variable declared in the transformed data block may be used in the model block. But a

> variable declared in the generated quantities block may not be used in any earlier block, including the model block."
>
> [There's one qualification I've noticed: variables in an earlier block are read-only for later blocks (with the
> exception of parameter sampling statements, which I'm aware are not the same sort of thing as conventional assignments).]

Right -- variables can only be assigned to (show up on the
left side of an "<-") in the block in which they are declared.

> However, *variables declared in the "model" block (even at its top level) are not in scope in the "generated quantities"
> block.* Accordingly, if I want to retrieve values of my calculated probabilities of choosing the better stimulus on each

> trial ("p_best" in the skeleton code below), I can't retrieve it from the "model" block, and if I declare it in an
> earlier block, I can't write to it from the "model" block -- so my only option is to recalculate it within the
> "generated quantities" block -- which is somewhat inefficient since I had to calculate it anyway as part of the model.
> (Not as inefficient as it could be, as I understand that the "generated quantities" block is executed less often than
> the "model" block -- but it's still noticeable.)

I'll try to clarify in the manual.

The variables in the model block are all local variables, which only persist
in the block in which they are defined.

To define a variable you need in the model block, use the
transformed parameter block.

> *Could "model" variables be put in read-only scope for the "generated quantities" block* (clearly, with the caveat that

> only variables declared in the "generated quantities" should be reported back to e.g. RStan or the final output, or

> there'd be too much junk coming back in many cases -- but a simple copy would suffice, e.g.: *generated quantities {
> real my_copy; my_copy <- my_model_var; }*)?

The could be, but they're not going to be :-)

> Or is there some other obvious way of retrieving posterior distributions of things calculated within the model block
> that I've not seen?

Yes, put them in the transformed parameter block.

> Simplest code to reproduce is:
>
>      model {
>          real modelthing;
>          modelthing <- 1.0;
>      }
>      generated quantities {
>          real thing;
>          thing <- modelthing;
>      }
>
> ... generates error:
>          thing <- modelthing;
>                  ^-- here
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> variable "modelthing" does not exist.
>
> More realistic skeleton code below.

In this case, you'd do this:

transformed parameters {

   real modelthing;
   modelthing <- 1.0;
}

Then modelthing is available in the model and will
also be printed.

If the variable being defined does not depend on any parameters (implicitly,
this includes other transformed parameters or local variables), as
in this example, then it's more efficient to define it in the transformed data block.

- Bob

That's an interesting idea.  We could make it
an option and spit it out as another "parameter".
It'll take a bit of work on the code generator side
and on the command side, but it's not that big a deal.

Do we really care about it, though?

I don't want to just add features because we can.  The
combinatorics of their interactions will inevitably weigh down future
development unless they can be neatly factored.

 > Then the difference between that and
 > the last draw gives the constants collectively, which could then retroactively
 > be added to all realizations of lp__ if
 > normalized calculations are needed.

The regular versions of lp__ also include the Jacobian adjustments,
because they're on the unconstrained scale.

I think a final log prob value would be more useful for users
on the natural model scale.  But then we couldn't just do the
clever diff.

I've also been thinking we could instead of a single
model block have a model that separated the likelihood and
prior terms.  Then we could do something more like DIC.
The issue there is that DIC also wants the value of the log
likelihood at the posterior mean, which isn't easy to get
within Stan.  It could be done on the R side by calculating
the mean and then feeding that back into the model.  It
could even be done by a user now that we can access the log
prob function directly.

- Bob

Thanks, I've implemented what you've suggested. At least the parts I understand. It's now usually close to what I get with R's arima (with xreg) now, but then there are times where it's obviously different.

And as I've thought about it, I think the problem is that the normal distribution is symmetric, so whatever I do with the scale will increase the spread but won't push it in one direction or another. Which an AR(1) noise would do, I think: tend to push things in one direction for a while, then another (positive AR coefficient), or back and forth (negative AR coefficient). So whether I constrain kappa or use fabs or whatever, the AR(1) noise is too free to move "the wrong way". At least that's how I think it works.

So my guess is that the model works well when the AR coefficient it positive and not so well when it's negative. I've thought about using a beta distribution, scaled appropriately to extend outside of [0,1], but it's pretty complicated to imagine how to make everything work appropriately.

> (Does somebody want to take a whack at writing up all of
> this stuff (DIC, Bayes Factors, etc. etc.) for the manual?

I'm happy to write something up about Bayes factors/model evidence but I don't feel comfortable quite yet with the various information criterion to talk about them with any generality (they're not hard to present as definitions, but the assumptions that go into them are often hard to understand).

Most importantly, NEVER try to calculate the model evidence using posterior draws.  You're essentially calculating the Monte Carlo estimate of the function f(alpha) = 1, which has infinite Monte Carlo variance -- it's the one estimate you can't get with MCMC alone.  Stable, accurate estimates of the evidence require more sophisticated techniques like nested sampling which could be coded in Stan only after adding some new features (non-holonomic, multivariate constraints -- this is where bouncing is a requirement).

-Mike

I have no idea.  Andrew's been spending a lot of time
thinking about these things, so I can ask him during
the meeting.

 > In other
> words, can't they just do (some) model comparisons on the unbounded parameter space if they add the constants back in?

I don't know where the parameterization is going to matter.
I'd think it'd all just cancel out if the measures made sense.

> As to whether people want to print an lp__ with or without constants, I don't think they should care. But it would be
> kind of useful to be able to compare with a log-likelihood that is calculated in R, which would include the constants.

In general, a Stan model only defines a quantity proportional
to the log posterior up to an additive constant.  You'd have to define
the log likelihood explicitly to be assured to get it.  Even if you
the specification was of a log joint, you'd need to separate
the calculations of the prior and likelihood.

The comparison calcs under DIC additionally require
the model log likelihood at the posterior mean.  And for WAIC,
we need the log likelihoods of individual data points.

So I think the jury's still out on how best to do all of this.

It was rstan.

I should have made notes but from recollection I have copied and updataed Tony Breyal's Windows R/Rcpp install tips <http://tonybreyal.wordpress.com/2011/12/07/installing-rcpp-on-windows-7-for-r-and-c-integration/>

Keith

The Solution

It turns out that there’s two issues here:

(1) the cygwin warning which we can ignore as it has nothing to do with Rcpp and is caused by using the 64bit version of MinGW from Rtools when adding it to our PATH variable (easily solved by choosing the 32bit version instead, shown below in step 5 part viii)

(2) the actual Rcpp issue itself which happened because I had originally installed R on a path with a space in it. In fact (and this is something I didn’t previously know) it’s officially recommended that one does not install R on Windows with a path containing a space (see rw-FAQ 2.2).

So armed with this knowledge, here is how I got Rcpp working from beginning to end (a lot of the sub-steps below are blindingly obvious but I included them anyway for the sake of completeness in case other people with similar problems come across this post):

Install R on a path that does not contain a space.

(i) download R from: http://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/

(ii) double click the downloaded .exe file

(iii) press Run when the security warning appears

(iv) press Yes when the User Account Control message box appears

(v) Choose your language (I choose English)

(vi) when prompted for where to install R, choose a location without a space. I choose "C:\R\R-2.14.0″

(vii) click Next on all following screens to finish installation (I left the defaults unaltered).

.

Install Rtools for components necessary to buld R (this has the tool chain require for C++ code compilation)

(i) Go to this webpage: http://probability.ca/cran/bin/windows/Rtools/

(ii) In the downloads section, choose a compatible version for your version of R e.g. Rtools30.exe

(iii) press Run when the security warning appears

(iv) press Yes when the User Account Control message box appears

(v) choose your language (I choose English)

(vi) choose where to install (I chose "C:\R\Rtools" and full installation with path changes)

(vii) click Next on all following screens to finish installation (I left the defaults unaltered).

(viii) read http://probability.ca/cran/bin/windows/Rtools/Rtools.txt carefully and intall Inno Setup installer from http://www.innosetup.com

and MinGW packages, obtained from http://sourceforge.net/projects/mingw/files/

Download batchfiles to always point to the latest version of R on your system when running R from the command line (I have found that this saves a lot of time in the long run)

(i) go to: http://cran.r-project.org/contrib/extra/batchfiles/

(ii) choose the latest version (I chose batchfiles_0.6-6.zip)

(iii) when downloaded, right click on file and click Extract All.

(iv) click Browse and choose where you want to put the extracted folder (I chose "C:\R\")

.

Download Redmond Path Utility to alter PATH variables in a very user friendly fashion:

(i) go to: http://download.cnet.com/Redmond-Path/3000-2094_4-10811594.html

(ii) click on "Download Now CNET Secure Download"

(iii) double click the downloaded .exe file

(iv) press Run when the security warning appears

(iv) press Yes when the User Account Control message box appears

(v) press Next

(vi) press Decline (unless you want the annoying advertising extra).

(vii) click open

(viii) An explorer window will open with RedmondPath.zip

(ix) click Extract All.

(x) click Browse and choose where you want to put the extracted folder (I chose "C:\R\")

.

Edit PATH variable to allow system wide access to the current version of R on the computer and components of Rtools

(i) double click the Redmond Path Utility from step 4 above (mine is in: "C:\R\RedmondPath\Redmond Path.exe")

(ii) click Yes when the User Account Control message box appears

(iii) click the green "+" icon in the top left corner so we can add elements to the PATH variable

(iv) In the window which pops open, navigate to "C:\R\batchfiles_0.6-6″ and click OK

(v) click the green "+" icon in the top left corner so we can add elements to the PATH variable

(vi) In the window which pops open, navigate to "C:\R\Rtools\bin" and click OK

(vii) click the green "+" icon in the top left corner so we can add elements to the PATH variable

(viii) In the window which pops open, navigate to "C:\R\Rtools\MinGW\bin" and click OK

.

Restart your computer (this solved an issue where the edits to the PATH variable above had not taken immediate affect)

.

Open R and run the following code

# install packages

install.packages(c("Rcpp", "rbenchmark", "inline", "Runit"))

# load main two packages

library(Rcpp)

library(inline)

# do something with Rcpp to quickly check that it works

body <- '

NumericVector xx(x);

return wrap( std::accumulate( xx.begin(), xx.end(), 0.0));'

add <- cxxfunction(signature(x = "numeric"), body, plugin = "Rcpp")

x <- 1

y <- 2

res <- add(c(x, y))

res

On Monday, March 11, 2013 3:34:52 PM UTC-4, Keith O'Rourke wrote:
> (2) the actual Rcpp issue itself which happened because I had originally installed R on a path with a space in it. In fact (and this is something I didn’t previously know) it’s officially recommended that one does not install R on Windows with a path containing a space (see rw-FAQ 2.2).
>
> So armed with this knowledge, here is how I got Rcpp working from beginning to end (a lot of the sub-steps below are blindingly obvious but I included them anyway for the sake of completeness in case other people with similar problems come across this post):
>
> Install R on a path that does not contain a space.

I installed rstan successfully on 31 out of 32 Windows laptops last week (and I think the failure was due to a bad disk). Technically, it isn't necessary for R itself to be installed in a path that has no spaces, but Rcpp needs to be installed in a path that has no spaces. And by default, packages are installed in R_HOME\library so if R_HOME has spaces in it, then Rcpp will fail. So if you can't or don't want to reinstall R, you just need to change R's settings so that packages are installed in a directory without spaces. This involves the .Rprofile and / or .Renviron configuration files, which are documented under help(Startup). Then install Rcpp, inline, and rstan.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Meaning of lp__ and model complexity
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Meaning of lp__ and model complexity
messages.body_plain:
Hi, just a few things.
1.  I think the marginal probability of the data is overrated.  And it's basically meaningless when people use flat priors (all those N(0,100000) things that people keep sending us).
2.  Mike's right that you can't compute p(y) from the simulations.  What you can do (sometimes) is compute p(y|M1)/p(y|M2) based on simulations from model 1 and simulations from model 2 (that's called bridge sampling in statistics and something else in physics) and to compute relative values of p(y|M), where "M" is some continuously-parameterized family of models (that's called path sampling in statistics and I-don't-know-what in physics, and has connections to simulated tempering).
3.  BIC is not p(y).  BIC is bullshit (as Ben might say, and I agree with his phrasing on this one).
4.  Right now I prefer WAIC to DIC.  There's also cross-validation.  All these require additional info to subdivide the data into pieces (or, in the case of DIC, to subdivide data from parameters and to feed in a point estimate).
A

>>      > the last draw gives the constants collectively, which could then retroactively
>>      > be added to all realizations of lp__ if
>>      > normalized calculations are needed.
>>
>>    The regular versions of lp__ also include the Jacobian adjustments,
>>    because they're on the unconstrained scale.
>>
>>    I think a final log prob value would be more useful for users
>>    on the natural model scale.  But then we couldn't just do the

>

> the meeting.
>
> > In other
>> words, can't they just do (some) model comparisons on the unbounded parameter space if they add the constants back in?
>
> I don't know where the parameterization is going to matter.
> I'd think it'd all just cancel out if the measures made sense.
>
>> As to whether people want to print an lp__ with or without constants, I don't think they should care. But it would be
>> kind of useful to be able to compare with a log-likelihood that is calculated in R, which would include the constants.
>
> In general, a Stan model only defines a quantity proportional
> to the log posterior up to an additive constant.  You'd have to define
> the log likelihood explicitly to be assured to get it.  Even if you
> the specification was of a log joint, you'd need to separate
> the calculations of the prior and likelihood.
>
> The comparison calcs under DIC additionally require
> the model log likelihood at the posterior mean.  And for WAIC,
> we need the log likelihoods of individual data points.
>
> So I think the jury's still out on how best to do all of this.
>
> - Bob

Bob,

I posted something a bit less-than-helpful a couple of minutes ago and attempted to delete it, but wasn't able to. Sorry for the spam!

I created a test case:

sa <- arima.sim (list (ar=c(0.7), order=c(1, 0, 0)), 1000) + seq (0.5, 500, 0.5)
plot (sa)
stan.list1 <- list (N=length (sa), x=1:1000, y=sa)

stan.model1 <- stan (model_code=stan.code1, model_name="sa", data=stan.list1, iter=20000, chain=4)

print (stan.model1, digits_summary=8)

Which has a slope of 0.5 and an intercept of 0, with AR(1) noise and an AR coefficient of 0.7. With STAN, I got reasonable results:

              mean    se_mean         sd
alpha   -0.1293778 0.00181275 0.21566235
beta     0.5004723 0.00000317 0.00037522
kappa    0.6980644 0.00021365 0.02354209

The Rhat's were all less than 1.0002 which is a good sign as well.

In case the system did manage to delete my previous posting (which was basically the same, except with a regression intercept and slope of zero which is not very visible), you have my permission to use my example code however you want. On 3/11/13 10:07 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, March 11, 2013 9:05:45 PM UTC-4, Sedat wrote:
>
>     I can obtain results for only objects listed in parameters section of Stan syntax. How can I get the results for
>     something, that is transformed parameters, I put in the model section of the syntax? When I put these into
>     parameters section It gives an error which says you cannot declare the same thing twice. Let me be more specific.
>     For example in my syntax I want to get results for AIC and BIC. I put these and their formula into model statement.
>     I could not find a way to see these on my output. I tried to put them into transformed parameters statement just
>     after model statement, RStan did not let me do that. When I put transfromed parameters before model statement with
>     AIC and BIC declaration, it did not calculate the desired statistics because these 2 declarations require some
>     parameters from model and to be declared before these statements.
>
>
> It doesn't work to declare something in the transformed parameters block and define it in the model block? If not, you

> could possibly move the pieces that you need to calculate the AIC or BIC with from model to transformed parameters.s

Nope -- variables can only be set in the block in
which they're defined.

But you can always move any computation you want to
save into transformed parameters itself, because
even in the model, everything must be defined in
terms of the parameters and data.

- Bob

messages.subject: LaTeX hyperref index in Stan manual?
messages.subject_clean: LaTeX hyperref index in Stan manual?
messages.body_plain:
Does anyone know how to fix our LaTeX so that the
index entries are hyperlinked back to the pages on
which they occur?

The dev team's stumped;  I've personally spent an
embarassing amount of time trying different alternatives
to no avail.

The style file's in

  $stan/src/docs/stan-reference/stan-manuals.sty

and there's an auxiliary style file in the same
directory in file:

   stan-reference.ist

There seem to be all kinds of bad interactions with hyperref
and with makeidx.  And I've made it even more conufsing by
going through a LaTeX macro to auto-generate the index with
headings, subheadings, and styles.

I'd be happy to change our indexing format or the package
on which it depends if that's what it takes.

I'd be happy to hear hints as well as complete solutions,
but please don't just point me in the general direction of
TUG or the hyperref doc, both of which I've studied in depth.

Thanks!

- Bob

P.S.  I'm also happy to send anyone who fixes this problem
       a Stan t-shirt (S, L, XL, or 2XL left).  And I'll thank you
       in the manual acknowledgments, but that's just common
       courtesy.

P.P.S.  I need to figure out how to set up a shop so people can
         buy the T-shirts.  Or hats.  Or mugs.  Suggestions
         appreciated.  We ordered from CustomInk, who are great,
         but they don't set up storefronts like Cafe Press, etc.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Fellow Stan Users,

Using RStan (Stan 1.2.0, R 2.15.2, Mac OS X 10.6, RStudio 0.97.318), I'm trying to fit the parameters of a simple negative binomial model. Here's the Stan code:

data {
    int N;
    int y[N];
}

parameters {
    real<lower=0> alpha;
    real<lower=0> beta;
}

model {
    // alpha ~ uniform(0,1000);

messages.body_plain:
You need a prior on alpha and beta to keep them from
running off to infinity.  Here's the sample model distributed
in src/models/basic_estimators/negative_binomial.stan:

data {
   int<lower=1> N;
   int<lower=0> y[N];

}
parameters {
   real<lower=0> alpha;
   real<lower=0> beta;
}
model {

   alpha ~ cauchy(0,10);
   beta ~ cauchy(0,10);

   for (i in 1:N)

     y[i] ~ neg_binomial(alpha, beta);
}

Those are pretty fat priors -- you should use
something reasonable for what you expect alpha and beta
to be.

And keep in mind our negative binomial has the parameterization
like the gamma-Poisson in Andrew's book Bayesian Data Analysis
(formula's in the manual).

- Bob

> Stan 1.2.0 and RStan 1.2.0 are now available for download.
> See:
>
>      http://mc-stan.org/
>
> Here are the highlights.
>
>
> 1.  Full Mass Matrix Estimation during Warmup
>
> Yuanjun Gao, a first-year grad student here at Columbia (!),
> built a regularized mass-matrix estimator.   This helps
> for posteriors with high correlation among parameters
> and varying scales.  We're still testing this ourselves, so
> the estimation procedure may change in the future.
>
> It's not the default option.  The major reason is the matrix
> operations required are expensive, raising the algorithm
> cost to O(K * M * N^2 + log(M) N^3), where K is the average
> number of leapfrog steps, M is the number of iterations, and
> N is the number of parameters.
>
> Yuanjun did a great job with the Cholesky factorizations
> and implemented this about as efficiently as is possible.
> (His homework for Andrew's class was also the inspiration
> for the Gaussian process models in the manual.)
>
> It's integrated with NUTS.
>
>
> 2.  Cumulative Distribution Functions
>
> The practical upshot is that Stan supports more truncated
> distributions, and hence more truncated and censored data models.
>
> Michael Betancourt did the heavy lifting here, which involved a crazy
> amount of "special function" derivative calculations and implementations.
> Everyone knows that the derivative of a distribution function with respect
> to the variate is the density.  But what about the partials with respect to the other
> parameters?  We'll be documenting all of the functions and derivatives
> in the manual.
>
> Daniel Lee generalized the entire density and distribution function
> testing framework to generate code for tests.  We're doing much more
> extensive tests of the vectorizations and derivatives.  Also, Daniel
> implemented efficient vectorized derivatives for many more of the density
> functions.
>
>
> 3.  Model Log Probability and Derivatives in R
>
> Jiqiang Guo, who's at the helm of RStan, wrote code to allow users
> to access the log probability function in a Stan model and its gradients
> directly.  The functions are parameterized with the unconstrained
> parameterization of a Stan model with support on all of R^N.  He
> also exposed the model functions to convert back and forth between
> the constrained and unconstrained parameterizations for initialization
> and interpretation of the samples.
>
> David Blei suggested that if we added this feature, people
> could do interesting things in R with it, such as optimization.
> Let us know if you find it helpful.
>
>
> 4.  Print Posterior Summary Statistics from Command Line
>
> Daniel Lee wrote a program to print a summary of one or more chains
> from the command line, mirroring the print() command of RStan.
>
>
> 5.  Bug Fixes
>
> We also fixed a bad memory leak in multivariate operations that
> was introduced in the last release when we optimized the matrix
> operations for derivative calculations.  We also fixed the Windows
> issue with conservative matrix resizing which caused multivariate
> models to crash under Windows at optimization levels above 0.
>
>
> There's also been a lot going on in various branches that haven't
> been merged into the trunk yet, so stay tuned.
>
> - Stan Development Team
>
>
> P.S.  Here are the release notes.
>
>

> * command-line program to display output from multiple chains

half for R-hat and uses an R-hat-like variance estimator
for effective sample size, which is more conservative
for poorly mixed chains than others.
