I'm excited to be getting involved with stan finally.  I've done a few
simple models, mostly duplicating what's in the documentation, and now
I'm trying a mixture model and having difficulty.

This is essentially the model from the manual with a bit of fake data:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Generate data
require(rstan)
lambda <- 0.6
nsamp <- 1000
n1 <- floor(lambda * nsamp)
n2 <- nsamp - n1
mu1 <- 900
mu2 <- 1100
sigma1 <- 20
sigma2 <- 40
data <- c(rnorm(n1,mu1,sigma1), rnorm(n2,mu2,sigma2))
sdata <- data/1000
ndata <- rescale(data)
mdata <- data.frame(
                    idx=1:nsamp,
                    data=data,
                    sdata=sdata,
                    ndata=ndata)

## Set up model
mixmodel <- '
data {
  int<lower=1> K; // # components
  int<lower=1> N; // # points
  real<lower=0> y[N]; // data
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta;  // mixing proportions
  real<lower=0> mu[K]; // location
  real<lower=0,upper=3> sigma[K]; // scale
}
model {
  real ps[K];
  for (k in 1:K) {
    mu[k] ~ normal(0,3)T[0,];
  }
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K) {
      ps[k] <- log(theta[k])
               + normal_log(y[n],mu[k],sigma[k]);
    }
    lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(ps);
  }
}
'
mixdata <- list(K = 2, N = 1000, y = mdata$ndata)
fit.mix <- stan(model_code = mixmodel, data = mixdata,
                iter = 10000, chains = 4, verbose = FALSE)

First, I'd highly recommend just running a model for a few
iterations, then for a few more, and making sure it's
at least not crashing or getting stuck before going on
to days-long runs.

Second, you're right that we don't have an elementwise
division operator ./ defined for a real x and vector y.
It should behave like this:

    (x ./ y)[n] = x ./ y[n]

Is that what MATLAB does?

It makes sense to me -- what do others think?

It's certainly easy enough to implement.

We don't need the broadcast multiplication x .* y
because this is just the same thing as regular matrix
multiplication by a scalar, x * y.

We also don't have matrix divison by a scalar.  Should
that be for matrix (or vector) m and real x,
m / x or m ./ x?

- Bob

Thanks for the advice. The sampling finished last night, but as I expected the effective sample size/r_hat is far from satisfactory, and it created a stan object occupying 8GB of my RAM (I ran 4 chains with 1000 iterations each). Don't know what to do yet...

As for the MATLAB counterpart, I think y ./ x will do the thing, where y is a number and x is a vector. MATLAB also has an explicit broadcast function bsxfun. But in this case, I think y / x, which is interpreted as broadcast, would be better, because "." means "element-wise" to many people, which implies both arguments are vectors. Anyway, it's just my thought.

I also noticed that in FAQ about speeding up the code, there mentions that instead of doing (where y is a N*K matrix):

for (k in 1:K) {

    for (i in 1:N) {
        y[i,k] ~ normal(0, 1);
    }
}

A much faster way would be:

y ~ normal(0,1);

However, in my model, we have a matrix<lower=0>[F, K] D and I wrote:

log(D) ~ normal(0, 1);
or
D ~ lognormal(0, 1);

It gave me a syntax error on both. And just now, I found that it seems that transpose operator (') doesn't work in RStudio, as it kept asking me to enter another ' to balance. If there is any misunderstanding of the usage, please let me know.

Best,
Dawen

messages.body_plain:
On 3/17/13 7:58 PM, Dawen Liang wrote:
> Thanks for the advice. The sampling finished last night, but as I expected the effective sample size/r_hat is far from
> satisfactory,

This might be for other reasons.

If you tell us more about your model, we might be
able to suggest something.

> and it created a stan object occupying 8GB of my RAM (I ran 4 chains with 1000 iterations each). Don't
> know what to do yet...

How many parameters did you have such that 4 chains of 1K
iterations took 8GB of RAM?  Is that in RStan or using the
new command from the command-line to calculate R-hat and ESS
and whatnot?

For memory, you can stream the data out to file rather than saving
it.  The command-line version streams, and I believe
RStan is set up to turn off internal saving and turn on
streaming (someone else will know how to do it if possible).

You might want to try a smaller version of the model or
less data until you're confident it's all working, then turn
it loose on more data.

> As for the MATLAB counterpart, I think y ./ x will do the thing, where y is a number and x is a vector. MATLAB also has
> an explicit broadcast function bsxfun. But in this case, I think y / x, which is interpreted as broadcast, would be
> better, because "." means "element-wise" to many people, which implies both arguments are vectors. Anyway, it's just my
> thought.

The problem in my mind is that we already use / for
matrix division.  And this isn't a matrix division
operation, which would be y / x = y * inv(x).

I guess it's going to be confusing either way.

> I also noticed that in FAQ about speeding up the code, there mentions that instead of doing (where y is a N*K matrix):
>
> for (k in 1:K) {
>      for (i in 1:N) {
>          y[i,k] ~ normal(0, 1);
>      }
> }
>
> A much faster way would be:
>
> y ~ normal(0,1);

Sorry about that.

The FAQ got ahead of what we've implemented.
We've only vectorized probability functions for vectors,
row vectors and 1D arrays.  We will be doing matrices
and general arrays in the very near future (we just
laid the metaprogramming groundwork in the code last week).

For now, the best you can do is:

 >      for (i in 1:N) {

 >          y[i] ~ normal(0, 1);

It's probably not worth flattening the matrix into a
single size (F * K) array at this point, but it's possible
with some index fiddling.

> However, in my model, we have a matrix<lower=0>[F, K] D and I wrote:
>
> log(D) ~ normal(0, 1);
> or
> D ~ lognormal(0, 1);

These two things are not at all the same.  We work through
this very example in section 16.2 of the manual.

> It gave me a syntax error on both.

Right.  Until we add matrices to our vectorization,
it needs to be:

    for (f in 1:F)
      D[f] ~ lognormal(0,1);

It's a bit more efficient here (for now, until we vectorize)
to just declare it as an array,

   real<lower=0> D[F,K];

or an array of vectors,

   vector<lower=0>[K] D[F];

The reason is that we can then save an allocate/copy
step for D[f].

 >  And just now, I found that it seems that transpose operator (') doesn't work in
> RStudio, as it kept asking me to enter another ' to balance.

Is that in an editor?  Or was it in feeding the
model in as a string argument somewhere?  (I don't
like the latter practice -- I think it makes more sense
to keep the models in their own files, but I seem
to be in the minority with this opinion.)

> If there is any misunderstanding of the usage, please let
> me know.

No, it's an apostrophe for transpose.

I have no idea what's up with RStudio.  You could always put the
model in another file and just call it by name from the stan()
command.

- Bob

Vectorizing over 2-dimensional structures in "deep interactions" model?

------------------------------------------------------------

Hey guys,

I'm running a "deep interactions" model, i.e. similar to what Andy and I just published in AJPS -- code below.  This time I'm (a) using Stan via rstan, and (b) fitting a much bigger model with more groups and more interactions.  I am successfully fitting the model, but it's taking a *very* long time, on the order of ~4 days to fit.  I'm wondering if I can do some extra vectorization to speed it up.  Code is attached.  Any suggestions?

Some specifics that I can point out:

I'm fitting a logit with ~30,000 cases after missing value imputation.  There are 16 continuous variables, all rescaled to mean = 0, sd = 0.5 (the z_ variables).  There are 9 sets of group-level variables, all 9 of which are interacted with each other, in the form of varying intercepts.  Most of the groups have < 5 levels, with a couple of exceptions.  In particular:

n_sex = 2
n_eth = 4
n_inc = 5
n_mar = 2
n_edu = 2
n_age = 4
n_pid = 3
n_prmd = 7
n_votes = 3

But the model gets big when I do all the two-way interactions between all of these.

I think the big computational slow-down comes in all the looping, but it's unclear to me how to avoid it.  There are two types of loops: (1) The "deep interactions" are all two-dimensional structures, so I think I have to go through these loops to set the normalization priors; (2) I think I have to set the varying intercepts (assigning alpha_groups) through this loop.  Is there any way to vectorize either of these steps?

I ran this once, 8 chains at 2500 iterations, parallelized over 8 cores.  Some of the chains finished relatively quickly, but the last chain finished about 4 days later.  Each core here is 2.00 GHz on a linux box where memory is not a problem, so I shouldn't be paging out.

Any tips on how to make this faster?  One thing I can do is upgrade stan -- I'm currently on rstan 1.1.0 -- but I think the real gains are through vectorization, or anything else you might suggest.  Any help is appreciated ... thanks!

Last thing, I saw that you ask for the sessionInfo() from R.  I'm pasting it here, from the moment before I run the full model.

Bill Harris <bill_...@facilitatedsystems.com> writes:

> The model compiles and runs now.  I just have to figure out how to get
> sufficient mixing on theta to attain convergence.

Now I've got a model initialization or formulaton question, not a Stan
usage question.  I've created the following mixture model and am trying
to fit the fake data that the script generates.  This script should
replicate the entire calculation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Generate data

require(YaleToolkit)
require(arm)
require(rstan)
require(ggplot2)
require(scales)

lambda <- 0.6
nsamp <- 1000
n1 <- floor(lambda * nsamp)
n2 <- nsamp - n1
mu1 <- 900
mu2 <- 1100
sigma1 <- 20
sigma2 <- 40

data <- c(rnorm(n1,mu1,sigma1), rnorm(n2,mu2,sigma2))
sdata <- data/1000
ndata <- rescale(data)
mdata <- data.frame(
                    idx=1:nsamp,
                    data=data,
                    sdata=sdata,
                    ndata=ndata)
rm(data)
rm(sdata)
rm(ndata)

## Set up model

mixmodel <- '
data {
  int<lower=1> K; // # components
  int<lower=1> N; // # points

  vector<lower=0>[K] alpha; // prior

  real<lower=0> y[N]; // data
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta;  // mixing proportions
  real<lower=0> mu[K]; // location
  real<lower=0,upper=3> sigma[K]; // scale
}
model {
  real ps[K];

  theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);

  for (k in 1:K)
    mu[k] ~ normal(0,3)T[0,];
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K) {
      ps[k] <- log(theta[k])
               + normal_log(y[n],mu[k],sigma[k]);
    }
    lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(ps);
  }
}
'

mixdata <- list(K = 2, N = 1000, alpha = 1*c(0.6,0.4), y = mdata$sdata)

fit.mix <- stan(model_code = mixmodel, data = mixdata,

                iter = 400, chains = 4, verbose = FALSE)
              ##  iter = 1000, chains = 4, verbose = FALSE)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

So far, I've been unsuccessful in getting the chains to mix, and theta
makes the biggest problem.

I've tried the advice in chapter 18 of BDA to make the parameters of
Dir() be proportional to the relative sizes of the thetas and their
magnitude be proportional to the strength of the prior distribution.
With the current formulation, the parameters match the chosen values of
theta in the fake data, and the coefficient can be used to scale them up
or down.

I've tried the coefficient equal to 0.1 (making the distribution
Dir(0.06, 0.04)), 1, 10, and 100.  I've also set alpha = c(1,1) and

messages.body_plain:
Yair -- I think you missed the attachment.
The mailing list can't handle .stan suffixes,
but if you append .txt, they'll go through.

By all means you should definitely upgrade to
the latest Stan.  We're making it much faster
as we go, and it's only the later releases that have
vectorized all the distributions.

Loops per se aren't a problem -- they're compiled.
But vectorizing probability functions can really help
because we optimize the gradient calcs at the same time
and it really cuts down on non-branch-predictable
virtual function calls.  So it helps to run a loop to
construct a vector to pass into a probability function.
The loop itself will hardly take any time at all if it
just does simple arithmetic or index fiddling.

 > I ran this once, 8 chains at 2500 iterations, parallelized over 8 cores.  Some of the chains finished relatively
 > quickly, but the last chain finished about 4 days later.

It also sounds like your model's a good candidate
for what Andrew's been asking for -- something that
will run by time rather than number of chains.   We
don't trust the chains that start in the weeds anyway.

On that note, one thing you can do is try init=0, which
is a much better starting point for regressions (unbounded
params init to 0, positive bounded params to 1, bounded
both way params init to the middle of their range).

I've been meaning to figure out what, if any, overhead
is added by RStan over the command line.  Jiqiang has things
sorted out now so you can dump data through RStan in a readable
to command-line-Stan format, then run the command-line Stan itself,
which streams output, and then read it back into R for analysis
with Stan (and anything else you want in R).

One of the things we saw slowing down this kind of model was
covariance matrix priors with 0.99 off-diagonal correlations.

- Bob

You probably want to put a prior on the scales sigma.

I was about to point you to the doc, when I realized
that the model there doesn't have a prior on sigma.
I'll go add it, because it usually helps with convergence
(even if not strictly necessary for the prior to be
proper).

Do you mean you have a problem getting the chains
of a mixture model to mix with each other?  That's
typical because mixture models are not identified. Do
you get the same answer but with reversed
indices?  The traceplots of theta[1] and theta[2]
dont' have enough resolutions for me to tell.

Also, you can replace all of this:

 >    for (k in 1:K)
 >      mu[k] ~ normal(0,3)T[0,];

with just

   mu ~ normal(0,3);

becuase the normal's vectorized and you don't need the
truncation if both location and scale are constants and
the variate mu is properly constrained.

Your data's well separated, so I don't imagine there's
going to be a problem finding the modes.

Why are you doing this:

 > mu1 <- 900
 > mu2 <- 1100
 > sigma1 <- 20
 > sigma2 <- 40
 >
 > data <- c(rnorm(n1,mu1,sigma1), rnorm(n2,mu2,sigma2))
 > sdata <- data/1000
 > ndata <- rescale(data)

rather than just taking mu = 0.9, mu2 = 1.1 and
sigma1 = 0.02 and sigma2 = 0.04?

You should be able to get away with a Dirichlet(2,2)
or even Dirichlet(1,1) distribution, but I'd stay away
from Dirichlet(0.06, 0.04) for a problem where you expect
both items to have some count.  If you don't include a prior
at all, it's equivalent to Dirichlet(1,1).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Maybe I should go to bed :-)  You have an implicit
uniform prior over the declared support of sigma, which
is proper here because the support is bounded.

Initialization will be at the halfway point, which is
still high (1.5) for your scaled down parameters with
sigma = 0.02 and 0.04.  Stan can usually figure this out,
but it will take extra time to adapt compared to
initializations that are closer to their true values.

- Bob

On 3/18/13 7:52 AM, Bill Harris wrote:
> Thanks, Bob, for all the suggestions.

> In this note, you asked (essentially) why I scaled the data the way I did.  My real data will be more like the 900 and

> but dividing by 1000 seemed similar while giving me numbers that sounded familiar.

Yes, that will work better.  Stan can figure out
the scaling during warmup, but it can slow down
convergence if the initialization is poor (not near
where the true parameter values are).

Also, it often happens with setting "default" priors.

> I'm still quite new to Dirichlet distributions, so your practical advice helps.  The reminders about vectorization help,
> too.

You might want to think about Beta(theta|a,b) first,
because Dirichlet is just the multivariate version.
It's a bit different because it's univariate, so you
only get the first component of the two, but you
can visualize the various distributions more easily.

The basic idea is that your prior should be fat (or
at least flat) where you expect the parameter values to
be, not the other way around, as you see in a Beta(0.01,0.01)
if you're expecting a value that's not near 0 or 1.

- Bob

> Thanks Bob for the tips and for reminding me about the support of the log probability function. I guess I should
> truncate some of the priors/hyperparameters declared in the model{} statement.
>
> I have been trying to reparameterize the log-normal distribution in terms of a unit log-normal distribution and separate
> mean and scale terms (after the example of the normal distribution in the manual). And yes, that's proper mind
> gymnastics, so for anyone else who is looking to reparameterize the lognormal distribution, here's what I tried:
>
> x ~ lognormal(mu_log,sigma)
>
> is equal to
>
> x.raw ~ lognormal(0,1)
> x <- exp(mu_log + log(x.raw)*sigma)
>
> or
>
> x.raw ~ normal(0,1)
> x <- exp(mu_log + x.raw*sigma)

Stan is more imperative than BUGS or JAGS, so
this approach won't work because  x is data.

Now that I say that, I realize the reparameterization
is unlikely to help here.

Also keep in mind that the mean of the distribution
lognormal(nu,tau) is exp(nu + tau^2/2).  This is
described here:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution

In particular, the variance plays into the mean because
of the skew (log normal, unlike the normal, is not symmetric).

> I'm not quite sure whether the last reparameterization also requires me also to specify the Jacobian of the transform,
> so perhaps someone can comment on this. This Jacobian stuff is really beyond me (I'm not a statistician or
> mathematician). I abandonned the approach altogether when the model went completely berserk. May give it another try
> later, once I have solved the other issues pointed out by Bob.

I feel your pain.  When the Stan project was starting,
I thought all the formulas for log normal and inverse gamma
and what not were wrong in Andrew's book because I didn't know
about Jacobians.

There's a fairly gentle intro in the transforms chapter of
the manual.  It might help if you're playing with lognormal
models.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
A couple things that will speed things up a bit.  First, all the lines like:

for (i in 1:n_sex) {
  alpha_sex_eth[i] ~ normal(0, sigma_sex_eth);
  ....
}

Can just be:

alpha_sex_eth ~ normal(0, sigma_sex_eth);

Also, in general, when you have things that look like a*b + c*d + ...

It is faster to create two temporary vectors v1 = [a, c, ...] and v2 =
[b, d, ...] and replace the expression with dot_product(v1,v2)

Along a similar vein, if you're adding a lot of things up (a + b + c +
d + ...), it can sometimes be faster to create a temporary vector v =
[a, b, c, d, ...] and write sum(v).

Basically, in Stan copying is cheap but operations are expensive so
saving operations either by caching and reusing computations or using
single vector operations in place of multiple scalar operations will
generally make things much faster.

Cheers,
Marcus

P.S. It looks like you add alpha_sex_eth[sex[i_n], eth[i_n]]  twice,
I'm guessing this is a bug?

On 3/18/13 12:33 PM, Bill Harris wrote:
> Bob,
>
> I can't make your model run on my Windows box the way you sent it, and I'm not near a Linux box right now to test it there.

There shouldn't be a difference between the
way RStan runs under Windows or under Linux other
than the paths you use to refer to files.

> I modified your .R file to include the model definition a string called bobcmodel:
>
> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> N <- N1 + N2 + N3;
> mu1 <- -2.0;
> mu2 <- 0.5;
> mu3 <- 3.5;
> sigma1 <- 1.0;
> sigma2 <- 0.5;
> sigma3 <- 2;
>
> y <- c(rnorm(N1,mu1,sigma1),rnorm(N2,mu2,sigma2),rnorm(N3,mu3,sigma3));
>
> bobcmodel <- '
> data {
>     int<lower=1> K;
>     int<lower=1> N;
>     real y[N];
> }
> parameters {
>     simplex[K] theta;
>     real mu[K];
>     real<lower=0,upper=10> sigma[K];
> }
> model {
>     real ps[K];
>     mu ~ normal(0,10);
>     for (n in 1:N) {
>       for (k in 1:K)
>         ps[k] <- log(theta[k])
>                  + normal_log(y[n],mu[k],sigma[k]);
>       lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(ps);
>     }
> }
> '
>
> library("rstan");
> ## fit <- stan(model="normal_mixture_k.stan", iter=500, chains=1, init=0);
>
> ## fit <- stan(model_code = bobcmodel, iter=500, chains=1, init=0);
>
> ## fit <- stan(model_code = bobcmodel, data = list(K=K,N=N,y=y),iter=500, chains=1, init=0);
>
> ## fit <- stan(model = "normal_mixture_k.stan", data = list(K=K,N=N,y=y),iter=500, chains=1, init=0);
>
> ## fit <- stan(file="normal_mixture_k.stan", iter=500, chains=1, init=0);
>
> fit <- stan(file = "normal_mixture_k.stan", data = list(K=K,N=N,y=y),iter=500, chains=1, init=0);

 From the stan() doc in R:

   file
   A character string file name or a connection that R supports
   containing the text of a model specification in the Stan modeling
   language; a model may also be specified directly as a character
   string using parameter model_code or through a previous fit using
   parameter fit. When fit is specified, parameter file is ignored.

   model_code
   A character string either containing the model definition
   or the name of a character string object in the workspace.
   This parameter is used only if parameter file is not specified.
   When fit is specified, the model compiled previously is used so
   specifying model_code is ignored.

So its' file=model_file or model_code=model_string.

You need version 3 or 6, which correctly specify the
model and the data.

(Sorry if I said "model" at some point -- I keep doing
that in my own code and having to go back and look at the
doc.)

I think this might be easier if it were overloaded, where
we just say model=blah_blah_blah and RStan first sees
if that referes to a file, and if not interprets it
as a string.

> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> If I run it as you sent it, using the first stan() call, I get
>
>  > source("normal_mixture_k.R")
> Error in stan(model = "normal_mixture_k.stan", iter = 500, chains = 1,  (from normal_mixture_k.R#40) :
>    argument 1 matches multiple formal arguments

Right -- "model" isn't a defined key.
Apparently R lets you use prefixes of argument
names, which is why this error comes up.

> If I run the second stan() call (the one that references the model code rather than the model file), I get
>
>  > source("normal_mixture_k.R")
>
> TRANSLATING MODEL 'bobcmodel' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.

> C:/R/library/rstan/include//stansrc/stan/agrad/agrad.hpp:2190:17: warning: 'void stan::agrad::free_memory()' defined but
> not used [-Wunused-function]
> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) :
>    variable does not exist; processing stage=data initialization; variable name=K; base type=int
> failed to create the sampler; sampling not done

This also shouldn't run because you haven't specified the
data.  You either need an array of variable names to read
from the environment, or a list of variable definitions.

>  > K
> [1] 3
>

> not used [-Wunused-function]
> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) :
>    variable does not exist; processing stage=data initialization; variable name=K; base type=int
> failed to create the sampler; sampling not done

You need the data here.

> The sixth version works:
>
>  > source("normal_mixture_k.R")
>
> TRANSLATING MODEL 'normal_mixture_k' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
> COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'normal_mixture_k' NOW.

> In other words, I seem to need to pass in the data as an explicit list, not as globals, as you seemed to be able to do.

If the variables are defined in the global environment, you
should be able to pass in data using the argument

   data=c("K","N","y")

You can't just use c(K,N,y), because we need the names of
the variables as well as the data itself.

>   Furthermore, the argument of the file name on my Windows box is called "file", not "model".

That's true everywhere -- sorry if I said "model" at some point.

> I don't know if those are
> differences between Windows and other OSes or not.  The error message (especially the "argument 1 matches multiple
> formal arguments") weren't clear to me for a while.

No.

> Thanks for this, though.  Now I've got something that might help me with my inference challenge.

You're welcome.  Let us know if you have other issues.

- Bob

Thanks.  I saw the hidden R objects now, which are created by Rcpp in fact.  I do not know how/whether RCpp manages them.  RStan itself does not created any hidden objects.  The temporary file (dynamic shared object compiled from C++ code) can be seen for example as follows.

> acode <- 'parameters { real y;} model {y ~ normal(0,1);}'
> fit <- stan(model_code = acode)
.....
> get_stanmodel(fit)@dso
S4 class cxxdso: dso_saved = TRUE, dso_filename = file1b796de5b88b, size = 1.4 Mb.
And dso_last_path = '/var/folders/1x/sqww6q215t71967mr8ph987m0000gn/T//RtmpsrHs9Z/file1b796de5b88b.so'.
Created on: 'x86_64, darwin9.8.0' with 'CXXFLAGS =  -O3 $(LTO)     #set_by_rstan'.
Loaded now: YES.
The signatures is/are as follows:
$file1b796de5b88b
character(0)

For now, these files get created by RCpp, over which we do not have control.  We need to investigate if this is really annoying.  However, if we have a stanfit object say named fit and after I do the following

> fit <- stan(...)
> rm("fit")
> gc()
> getLoadedDLLs()

I could see that the compiled code were unloaded (i.e., not showing up from getLoadedDLLs).  So in the case, if we save the session, I do not think the hidden objects would refer to any object that is big.  Thus .RData file is not big.

Jiqiang

messages.body_plain:
In trying to replicate Nicolas's example, I ran into a
bug in Stan's code generator.   The following model can be parsed
by stanc, but the generated code causes the compilation
error reported below.

--------------------------------------------------------
data {
   vector[0] x;

}
parameters {
   real y;
}
model {
   y ~ normal(0,1);
}

--------------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------------
~/stan(master)$ mk ../temp4/zero
clang++ -I src -I lib/eigen_3.1.2 -I lib/boost_1.53.0 -Wall -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE
-DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS -Wno-unused-function -Wno-tautological-compare   -c -O0 -o ../temp4/zero.o ../temp4/zero.cpp
../temp4/zero.cpp:39:37: error: ambiguous conversion for functional-style cast from 'int' to 'vector_d'
       (aka 'Matrix<double, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>')
         x = std::vector<vector_d>(1,vector_d(0));
                                     ^~~~~~~~~~
lib/eigen_3.1.2/Eigen/src/Core/Matrix.h:220:34: note: candidate constructor
     EIGEN_STRONG_INLINE explicit Matrix(Index dim)
                                  ^
lib/eigen_3.1.2/Eigen/src/Core/Matrix.h:268:14: note: candidate constructor
     explicit Matrix(const Scalar *data);
              ^
1 error generated.
make: *** [../temp4/zero.o] Error 1
~/stan(master)$
--------------------------------------------------------

This is easy to fix -- we just need to use

   vector_d(Eigen::DenseIndex(0))

to resolve the overload and we're good to go.

But this wasn't the issue with Nicolas's model.
Zero-length arrays work as is, such as

    real x[0];

I/O also works OK for the command-line version of Stan,
where I wrote this for a data file.

--------------------------------------------------------
x <- c()
--------------------------------------------------------

So it doesn't look like the issue is in the basic Stan I/O.

I don't know what the right workaround is in R, but I'm confident
we (and by that I mean Jiqiang) will sort it out for the next release.

- Bob

P.S.  The Python interface for Stan is underway!  More on that later.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does NUTS fail?
messages.body_plain:
We would very much like to understand some of these
issues ourselves.

The technical issues in diagnosing convergence
presented by adaptive HMC/NUTS are the same as those
presented by Metropolis/Gibbs.

If you've already studied Radford Neal's MCMC handbook
chapter on HMC, you're well on your way to understanding
what's going on.  There's then the Hoffman and Gelman
paper on NUTS itself (also on arXiv, though it's about
to come out in JMLR).

The best thing to read next is Michael Betancourt's
arXiv papers on RM-HMC, which discusses the funnel example
(also discussed in the manual) in more detail.  The main
pathologies for HMC/NUTS have to do with complex posterior
geometries (high curvature and varying posterior scales).

HMC is rotation invariant (can handle high corelations)
but is not scale invariant (doesn't like badly conditioned
posteriors in the matrix sense).  Riemann Manifold HMC,
which we're working on now, is usually slower per iteration,
but can handle more complex posteriors.

Michael's also writing a package for diagnostics, which
should help with this, but isn't quite ready for prime
time (or so I understand --- correct me if I'm wrong here,
Michael).

What we're worried about is the case where the convergence
diagnostics like R-hat are consistent with convergence, but
the sampler hasn't actually converged.  One way Michael's
been suggesting dealing with this is to run NUTS, look
at the adapted step size and average (or max) tree depth,
then run basic HMC with a step size 1/2 the size and a
number of steps equal to 2^(depth + 1), where depth is
the max tree depth in the NUTS.  This should be substantially
slower, and perhaps require more iterations, but should give
the same answer.  If it does, the geometry's probably OK (right,
Michael?).

If you declare variables with constraints and the model
has support in the entire constrained space, then Stan will
deal with the transform to full support on R^N (perhaps for
a different N -- for instance, K-simplexes only need K-1 unconstrained
parameters because the last value is determined by 1 minus
the sum of the others).  There's a discussion of how this works
in the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does NUTS fail?
messages.body_plain:
First, let's distinguish between simulating Hamiltonian dynamics and NUTS, which uses those simulations to build up a binary tree from which a new point is sampled.

When can Hamiltonian dynamics fail?  While there are many failure cases, the most common involve the discretization step size being too large.  If the step size is too large everywhere in space then the dynamics quickly become chaotic and diverge, leading to very short trajectories.  If the step size is too large only for some parts of space, then the trajectory will not explore those regions and you can get biased samples.  The former is usually well controlled by adaptation algorithm, but failure would manifest as very small tree depths and high autocorrelations (small tree depths and small autocorrelations are okay).  The latter is more subtle -- if you want to be safe then run an auxiliary chain (starting at one of your nominal samples) but with 1/10 or 1/100 or the nominal adaptive step size (be careful that you're not hitting the max tree depth!  you might have to raise the threshold for these diagnostic chains).  Any failure would manifest as inconsistencies in these two samples -- visual examination is often sufficient, but you can run a KS test if you wanted to automate (implementing these kinds of tests in Stan is on the to-do list).  If you're model is hierarchical there can also be issues with limited potential variation -- see, for example, http://arxiv.org/abs/1212.4693).

So what about NUTS?  Formally NUTS never really fails, but it can terminate prematurely before reaching the optimal integration time.  This happens when the posterior is highly correlated and the spectral gap of the covariance is large (large spectral gap manifests has high frequency transverse oscillations which can trigger NUTS to terminate before the low frequency oscillations have a chance to move).  This can be diagnosed by looking at individual trajectories or, as above, seeing small tree depths but high autocorrelations.  Unfortunately there's nothing much that can be done without appealing to more advanced Hamiltonians, in particular one with a dense mass matrix (which you can conveniently use in Stan 1.2) or Riemannian HMC (coming soon).

We're working on some visual and automated diagnostics to catch these kinds of problems, but if you notice any weird behavior please don't hesitate to make a note of it on the list.

-Mike

messages.subject_clean: RStan Getting Started Guide: minor suggestion to speed up compilation speed
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stanisticians,

The RStan Getting Started Guide (https://code.google.com/p/stan/wiki/RStanGettingStarted) suggests bumping up compiler optimization level to -O3, by changing the line:

 CXXFLAGS = -g -O2 $(LTO)

but makes no mention of removing the -g flag (which includes debugging information in the compiled object code).  For normal Stan users, is there actually a purpose to keeping the debug info at all?

If I remove the -g, I consistently get about 20% faster compiles on my system (Mac OS X 10.6). I have not tested on other platforms, but I surmise that a suggested installation procedure should nudge the user towards the fastest default.

What's been the experience of others?

    + Nicolas

>

> [a, b, c, d, ...] and write sum(v).

> Basically, in Stan copying is cheap but operations are expensive so
> saving operations either by caching and reusing computations or using
> single vector operations in place of multiple scalar operations will

messages.body_plain:
On 3/21/13 6:08 AM, Lindsay wrote:
...

I found the original post -- don't know why I didn't see it
earlier.

First, modeling.  Are the zeroes really zeroes and not
missing data?  If they're missing data, you should model
the missingness rather than just including them in the
data.  If they're real, I'm not sure a simple regression is the
right model, because the data looks more like a mixture of zeroes
and a real trend.

Although you seem to be able to run 1M iterations (!!!), the
model can be made more efficient in two ways.  Here are the
original loops:

   mu_a_type1 ~ normal(5000, 100);
   for (k in 1:N_types) {

     a_type[k,1] ~ normal(mu_a_type1, sd_a_type1);

     for (t in 2:N_years)

       a_type[k,t] ~ normal(a_type[k,t-1], sigma_state[k]);
   }

Nice use of naming conventions, by the way -- I could understand
the model just by reading it.

To speed up the iterations without changing the model, you
can vectorize.  If you let a_type_tr be the transpose of a_type,
you can write the above loops in vectorized form as:

   a_type_tr[1] ~ normal(mu_a_type1, sd_a_type1);

   for (t in 2:N_years)

     a_type_tr[t] ~ normal(a_type_tr[t-1], sigma_state);

The vectorized versions are a lot faster.  If N_types is
small, the gains will be modest.  You could even go a step
further and vectorize the second call to normal by defining
a temporary.  It's the calls to normal that are slow, not
looping or assignments, and vectorizing speeds up the calls
to normal.

By using the "Matt trick", you can also speed up sampling in
terms of number of effective samples per iteration.  Working
from the vectorized code above, the Matt-ed out code would involve
a new raw parameter and would move a_type_tr to a transformed
parameter, with model code:

   a_type_tr_raw[1] ~ normal(0,1);

   for (k in 1:N_types)

     a_type_tr_raw[t] ~ normal(0,1);

and transformed parameter code:

   a_type_tr[1] <- a_type_tr_raw[1] * sd_a_type1 + mu_a_type1;

   for (t in 2:N_years)

     a_type_tr[t] <- a_type_tr_raw[t] * sd_a_type1 + a_type_tr[t-1];

You'd then use a_type_tr as before.

Having said all this, I really don't want to encourage people
to prematurely optimize.  If the model's already fast enough
to converge and sample once it converges, I wouldn't change it!

But if you want to do more groups or handle lots more data, the
above can really help.

- Bob

I forgot about that problem.

SD relies heavily on tabular descriptions of nonlinear functions; usually with uneven spacing of the argument.  I have tended to use the akima interpolation routine, but sometimes a linear or step interpolation is handy to match the results from some commercial software.

If odestan (!?) had those three routines in a suitably-licensed implementation, I'd be happy.  If it also had Stineman interpolation, I wouldn't argue. :-)

messages.body_plain:
Great answers! Thanks a lot.

I am really looking forward to seeing this diagnostic tools becoming easier to access. To be honest, since I got Stan I focus much more on my models and only take a look at any convergence if my Rhat is bad, but this usually means my model is crap. In that sense Stan really helped in the spirit of Andrew to focus on modeling, which is great.

As I am trained physicist I am wondering if Stan is automatically transforming stuff into easier geometries. I.e. I remember in my physics courses to always think long and hard about possible variable transformations before solving any problem. In fact, there are approaches out there which reformulate a given mechanics problem (which is what you solve by integrating equations of motion, right?) to write a partial differential equation system which finds a transformation turning a given problem into a set of trivially solvable differentials. The trick is always to identify Noether currents, i.e. constants of the equations of motion like total energy which corresponds to probability mass. However, there are more such constants at least in physical systems, such as conservation of angular momentum and the like. All this is quite apparent if one ever tried to solve Kepler problems in euclidian coordinates, rewriting it in angular coordinates makes life easier...

I am just curios  here, so does Stan take these things into account?

Best,
Sebastian

Ah, and to raise my vote here as well again: bringing ODEs into Stan would be really great.

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, March 23, 2013 5:44:24 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> As I am trained physicist I am wondering if Stan is automatically transforming stuff into easier geometries. I.e. I remember in my physics courses to always think long and hard about possible variable transformations before solving any problem.

There are a lot of automatic transformations in Stan that are not obvious to the user; i.e. all parameters declared with restrictions on their support are actually transformations of primitive unbounded parameters. Your general point about geometry is an important one, but it is mostly the responsibility of the user to choose a  (re)parameterization of the model that is easier to sample from. The example of the funnel in the manual is instructive, which can also be seen in RStan by doing

funnel_reparam <- stan_demo("funnel_reparam")
pairs(funnel_reparam, pars = c("x_raw[1]", "x_raw[2]", "y", "x[1]", "x[2]", "lp__"))

And there is a bunch of stuff in the Optimizing Stan Code part of the manual about reparameterizations that are usually intended to make the primitive parameter space closer to a spherical normal.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does NUTS fail?
messages.body_plain:
The Hamilton-Jacobi formalism you mention provides a construction for calculating the trivially-integrable action/angle variables, but only for integrable systems.  Unfortunately exactly integrable systems are rare, and the method will not prove useful for most HMC problems.  About the only exactly integrable systems would be derived from mixtures of Gaussians.

I've played around with trying to identify and utilize more symmetry, whether it be through Noether currents or Killing vectors, but these kinds of approaches always end up being very application specific.  As Bob notes, Riemannian HMC approximates the system as exactly integrable in a local neighborhood, which is about as best we can do in a general setting.

> b) the compiled command-line print.exe sometimes crashes when I try to print the samples.csv. I don't use R, so this
> function is GREAT! I can attach one of the problematic files?

Yes, please send us something that crashes.

> c) my pilot model currently uses a subset of ~600 respondents; even without respondent-specific beta parameters, there
> are ~1,200 parameters that need not be monitored (i.e. the s[] and s_star[] parameters). With respondent-specific
> parameters, there are ~ 14,000 parameters that need not be monitored. And with a real-life dataset with many more
> respondents, even many many more. So, is a new STAN feature that allows several parameters to be excluded from the
> samples.csv output a possibility? I've briefly mentioned this before, apologies for the duplication.

As I believe we've replied before, we're reluctant to do this
because of the implications for convergence monitoring.

> d) using an array in the likelihood declaration does not work (yet)?
> e) I've tried to replace the poisson with a categorical distribution. In BUGS this is coded as follows:
>
>    for (n in 1:N){
>     for (t in 1:T){
>      Y[n,t] ~ dcat(prob[n, t, 1:A])
>    }}
>
> I've tried several options,

You can use

   Y[n,t] ~ categorical(prob[n,t]);

in Stan.

but always got an error in the calculation of the probabilities when I initialized them as:
> vector[A] prob[N,T], which is -I think- the required form(?). A suggestion would be much appreciated!

You want a simplex if it's categorical probability.
Stan requires the constraints to be specified.  So that's

   simplex[A] prob[N,T];

I'd stay away from using variables named "prob" in a model!

> f) the multiplication of s[n] and beta[] is not fully identified, hence the mean-of-1 constraint on the s[n]. I don't
> understand, however, why the posterior mean of the s_star[n] are so much smaller than 1. Did I specify the constraint on
> mu_s incorrectly, or perhaps any other idea why?

I don't think the following does what you intend:

   parameters {
     ...
     vector[N] s_star;
   }
   transformed parameters{
     vector[N] s;
     s <- s_star/mean(s_star);
   }

   model {
     ...
     s_star ~ lognormal(-0.5 * square(sigma_s) , sigma_s);

First, you probably want a prior on sigma_s -- it's unbounded here.
I'd then expect sigma_s to go to zero anyway given the way you
set up the sampling distribution on s_star.  But what you really
want is something like a prior on the transformed parameter.  But
to do that you'll need to adjust for the Jacobian.

Or find some other way to identify the model.

- Bob

messages.subject: Does adaptation carry over from previous fit?
messages.subject_clean: Does adaptation carry over from previous fit?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

A quick question from a Stan newbie: If I first fit a model in R using stan and then pass that model fit to a second call of stan, should I re-adapt the model in the second call, or does the adaptation of the model carry over from the first call? If so, is there any value to a long warm-up in the first call? I am interested in this question generally, but in the specific application I am working on the second call to stan parallelizes chains across different cores. R code snippet below (stan code omitted due to its length):

n.chains <- 2
n.iter <- 1e5
n.warm <- 1e4

stan.fit <- stan(model_code=stan.code, data=stan.data, chains=1, iter=n.warm)

stan.par <- mclapply(1:n.chains, FUN=function(chain) {
  stan(fit=stan.fit, data=stan.data, iter=n.iter, chains=1, chain_id=chain,
               warmup=0, ## Is this okay to do?
       )})

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, March 25, 2013 4:35:15 PM UTC-4, Devin Caughey wrote:
> A quick question from a Stan newbie: If I first fit a model in R using stan and then pass that model fit to a second call of stan, should I re-adapt the model in the second call, or does the adaptation of the model carry over from the first call?

No, it is essentially starting over from scratch, just without the compilation overhead.

> If so, is there any value to a long warm-up in the first call?

Not much. If the model is working on a few iterations and has been optimized, then do a little warmup and get as many effective samples as you need for inference. If it hasn't converged, then extend both the warmup and the iterations, but in my experience it is amazing how quickly Stan converges on a lot of problems.

Ben

It's easy to implement.

We haven't yet vectorized categorical.  We really haven't
vectorized any of the distributions that have multivariate
parameters or outcomes.  Once we get everything fully
vectorized, you'll be able to write

   Y[n,t] ~ categorical( softmax(lambda[n,t]) );

as

Right now, you could vectorize this further:

 >        lambda[n,t,a] <- s[n] * dot_product(X[n,t,a], beta[n]);

but I don't really think it'll be worth doing.

In general, you can convert categorical to multinomial,
but it's not going to help you here because you have
varying distributions going into each call to categorical().

messages.subject: Vectorized Count Model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am fitting a binomial count model, where the counts are stored in R as a 3D array (group by question by time). The model runs fine in non-vectorized form, with the array of counts declared as follows:
  int<lower=0> RRY[G, Q, T]; // count of correct answers in group, by year
  int<lower=0> NNY[G, Q, T]; // count of responses in group, by year
and the response model written as follows:
  RRY[g, q, t] ~ binomial(NNY[g, q, t], prob[q, t, g]); // group counts
To speed up computation, I would like to vectorize binomial(), but this requires that I declare RRY and NNY as arrays of vectors, as in:
  vector[T] RRY[G, Q];
This causes an error, however, because binomial() requires that the response be integer type. I haven't come across any way to declare an integer vector, which makes me think that they are not supported. Is this correct? If so, is there any alternative way to vectorize this problem?

Thanks!
~Devin

> On 3/26/13 3:25 PM, Devin Caughey wrote:
> >
> > I am fitting a binomial count model, where the counts are stored in R as a 3D array (group by question by time). The
> > model runs fine in non-vectorized form, with the array of counts declared as follows:
> >
> >   int<lower=0> RRY[G, Q, T]; // count of correct answers in group, by year
> >   int<lower=0> NNY[G, Q, T]; // count of responses in group, by year
> >
> > and the response model written as follows:
> >
> >   RRY[g, q, t] ~ binomial(NNY[g, q, t], prob[q, t, g]); // group counts
> >
> > To speed up computation, I would like to vectorize binomial(), but this requires that I declare RRY and NNY as arrays of
> > vectors, as in:
> >
> >   vector[T] RRY[G, Q];
>
> Not quite.  Here's the signature for binomial (from
> the index):
>
>  binomial_log
>  (ints n, ints N, reals theta):real
>
> An "ints" type means it can be an int or an int *array*,
> and "reals" means it can be a real, real array, or real vector.
>
> You're right that there are no vectors of int types.
>
> There is a simple and then an extreme form of vectorization
> you could do for this statement:
>
>   RRY[g, q, t] ~ binomial(NNY[g, q, t], prob[q, t, g]); // group counts
>
> If you reorganize prob to be indexed prob[g,q,t], then you can
> vectorize on t:
>
>   RRY[g,q] ~ binomial(NNY[g,q], prob[g,q]);
>
> Or you could reorganize and vectorize on the longest dimension.
>
> At a more extreme level, you can create one large G * Q * T array
> and fill it in with your own indexing and vectorize that way.
> It'll be more efficient, despite all the copying, but less readable.
>
>   RRY_vec int[G * Q * T];
>   NNY_vec int[G * Q * T];
>   prob_vec real[G * Q * T];
>   int pos;
>   pos <- 1;
>   for (g in 1:G) {
>     for (q in 1:Q) {
>       for (t in 1:T) {
>         RRY_vec[pos] <- RRY[g,q,t];
>         NNY_vec[pos] <- NNY[g,q,t];
>         prob_vec[pos] <- prob[q,t,g];
>         pos <- pos + 1;
>       }
>     }
>   }
>   RRY_vec ~ binomail(NNY_vec,prob_vec);
>
> - Bob

You should not be getting a malloc error and crash no matter
what you do, so this is definitely a bug in our code somewhere.

Which version of RStan are you using?  I'd like to try to isolate
the problem as an issue in RStan vs. Stan itself.

Could you send along the whole model?  Feel free to send
it just to me (ca...@alias-i.com) if you don't want to share
with the world.  Data would help to, but I can do without that.

You don't want to have to put these local variables in the
transformed parameter block where they'll be saved.  You can
make them locals in one of two ways.  You can declare them at
the top of the model block, as in

model {

   int RRY_vec[T * Q * G];
   int NNY_vec[T * Q * G];
   int pos;

   ...compute values of RRY and NNY...
   RRY_vec ~ binomial(NNY_vec, prob_vec);
}

or they need to be enclosed in their own curly braces within
the model:

{

   int RRY_vec[T * Q * G];
   int NNY_vec[T * Q * G];
   int pos;

   ... compute values of RRY and NNY ...
   RRY_vec ~ binomial(NNY_vec, prob_vec);
}

The curly braces define a block which determines the scope and local variables;
local variables can only be declared at the top of a block.

- Bob

messages.subject: stochastic MAP in stan
messages.body_plain:
stanimaniacs,

thanks to the stan development team, implementing stochastic MAP
estimation in stan is easy. there was a little trickiness to getting
it to work, so i thought i'd share.

best
dave

---

you'll need

- a subsample(b) function that grabs a subsample of size b from your
  data set

- a stepsize(t) function that gets the t-th stepsize. (to start, you
  can even just choose a constant stepsize.)

here is a skeleton of the program:

# model_filename = stan model
# subsample(b)   = fun that returns a sample of b data points from the data
# n              = data set size
# batch_size     = size for each subsample to analyze on each iteration
# niter          = number of iterations
# stepsize(t)    = fun that returns the stepsize at iteration t
# model          = (opt) a pre-compiled model

stochastic.map <- function(model_filename, subsample, n, batch_size,
                           niter, stepsize, model = NULL)
{
  # compile the model (if needed) and initial parameters.
  # here, parameters are initialized to zero.

  if (is.null(model))
  {
    dummy_subsample <- sample.documents(data, batch_size)
    model <- stan(model_filename, data = dummy_subsample, chains=0)
  }
  nparams <- sum(unlist(model@par_dims))
  params <- rep(0, nparams)
  grad_scale <- n / batch_size

  # run stochastic gradient ascent by subsampling a batch, computing a
  # noisy gradient, and taking a step.  at each point, compute the
  # the per-data log probability as a score to track.

  score <- numeric(niter)
  for (t in 1:niter)
  {
    batch <- subsample(batch_size)
    iter_model <- stan(fit = model, data = batch, chains = 0)
    grad <- grad_scale * grad_log_prob(iter_model, params)
    params <- params + stepsize(t) * grad
    score[t] <- log_prob(iter_model, params) / batch_size
  }

  # return the model object (in case we want to run again)
  #        the params vector
  #        the score trajectory

  list(model = model, params = params, score = score)
}

messages.body_plain:
Once we've implemented black box VB, MAP will be a thing of the past.

On Mar 26, 2013, at 6:49 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:

> Dave, thanks for putting together stochastic MAP. What's really neat is how clean it is, once Stan has abstracted away the model and the gradients. It reads like pseudo-code.
>
> For users that are diving into Stan at this level, if you have suggestions / requests /improvements for the API, please feel free to bring it up.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
>
> On Tue, Mar 26, 2013 at 6:41 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> > Awesome!
> >
> >
> > On Tue, Mar 26, 2013 at 6:20 PM, David Blei <david...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > stanimaniacs,
> > >
> > > thanks to the stan development team, implementing stochastic MAP
> > > estimation in stan is easy. there was a little trickiness to getting
> > > it to work, so i thought i'd share.
> > >
> > > best
> > > dave
> > >
> > > ---
> > >
> > > you'll need
> > >
> > > - a subsample(b) function that grabs a subsample of size b from your
> > >   data set
> > >
> > > - a stepsize(t) function that gets the t-th stepsize. (to start, you
> > >   can even just choose a constant stepsize.)
> > >
> > > here is a skeleton of the program:
> > >
> > > # model_filename = stan model
> > > # subsample(b)   = fun that returns a sample of b data points from the data
> > > # n              = data set size
> > > # batch_size     = size for each subsample to analyze on each iteration
> > > # niter          = number of iterations
> > > # stepsize(t)    = fun that returns the stepsize at iteration t
> > > # model          = (opt) a pre-compiled model
> > >
> > > stochastic.map <- function(model_filename, subsample, n, batch_size,
> > >                            niter, stepsize, model = NULL)
> > > {
> > >   # compile the model (if needed) and initial parameters.
> > >   # here, parameters are initialized to zero.
> > >
> > >   if (is.null(model))
> > >   {
> > >     dummy_subsample <- sample.documents(data, batch_size)
> > >     model <- stan(model_filename, data = dummy_subsample, chains=0)
> > >   }
> > >   nparams <- sum(unlist(model@par_dims))
> > >   params <- rep(0, nparams)
> > >   grad_scale <- n / batch_size
> > >
> > >   # run stochastic gradient ascent by subsampling a batch, computing a
> > >   # noisy gradient, and taking a step.  at each point, compute the
> > >   # the per-data log probability as a score to track.
> > >
> > >   score <- numeric(niter)
> > >   for (t in 1:niter)
> > >   {
> > >     batch <- subsample(batch_size)
> > >     iter_model <- stan(fit = model, data = batch, chains = 0)
> > >     grad <- grad_scale * grad_log_prob(iter_model, params)
> > >     params <- params + stepsize(t) * grad
> > >     score[t] <- log_prob(iter_model, params) / batch_size
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   # return the model object (in case we want to run again)
> > >   #        the params vector
> > >   #        the score trajectory
> > >
> > >   list(model = model, params = params, score = score)
> > > }
> > >
> > >

> # n              = data set size

>   # compile the model (if needed) and initial parameters.
>   # here, parameters are initialized to zero.

>   {

>     model <- stan(model_filename, data = dummy_subsample, chains=0)
>   }
>   nparams <- sum(unlist(model@par_dims))

This is fine for some models. But log_prob and grad_log_prob are defined on the unconstrained parameter space.  The number of unconstrained parameters might be different from what is obtained here.  Function "get_num_upars" can be used instead, that is

nparams <- get_num_upars

>   params <- rep(0, nparams)
>   grad_scale <- n / batch_size

>   # the per-data log probability as a score to track.

>     iter_model <- stan(fit = model, data = batch, chains = 0)
>     grad <- grad_scale * grad_log_prob(iter_model, params)

>   }
>

> }

>
> but I don't really think it'll be worth doing.
>

> but it's not going to help you here because you have
> varying distributions going into each call to categorical().
>
> - Bob
>

> >
> > Hi Bob,

> > ...

> > for (a in 1:A)

> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stochastic Volatility Models
messages.body_plain:
On 3/28/13 1:25 PM, Carlos wrote:

> I am wondering how STAN deals with a non-linear model like a Stochastic Volatility (SV) one.

The same way it deals with all models -- converts the
model to a log probabilty function with gradients then
runs NUTS (or a simpler HMC) sampler.  :-)

Matt Hoffman used some simple stochastic volatility models
to test NUTS vs. HMC in the paper (which is about to
be published in JMLR):   http://arxiv.org/abs/1111.4246

> I attach here a stan file
> that describes an AR(2) process with SV (and other exogenous regressors), where the error term of the regression is
> parametrized as in Kim, Sephard and Chib (1998), that is,
>
> |
> exp(h(t)/2)*e(t),e(t)~N(0,1)
> |

Stan, like BUGS and JAGS, was designed to allow you to evaluate
different models.  So you could try the Kim et al. parameterization.
Though I couldn't quite parse the left side of your statement
because I was expecting a scalar output but you seem to have
a pair.

Reparameterizations can help with sampling speed in Stan,
especially if the prior scale (size of variance) or
geometry (shape of covariance) can be controlled.  There's
a chapter of the manual providing examples.

> The code compiles, and runs. However, I do not know if I am taking a too naive approach here and if the results that I
> am getting are not proper...

I'd start with some models for which you know what the
answer is, either because you simulated the data or you
have some other software that gave you the answer.  Then you
can be confident it's working and go on from there (though
continuing to check with simulated data's always a good practice).

> SV models are tricky, and usually people (including myself) focus on the approximations
> derived in Kim et al's paper, or, more recently, using particle filters. Is there any reason why it should not work in
> STAN? If it works, I think this is a great improvement...

Nope, no reason at all --- it's the kind of example for which
we built Stan.

There are lots of things you can do to speed this model up with
vectorization.

This looks wrong:

     for (n in 1:N)
       H1noise ~ normal(0, ETAs);

You're sampling the same variable, H1noise, repeatedly.   Given that
it's a vector, you probably just want to drop the for wrapper.

For the truncation case:

     ar2 ~ normal(0,100) T[-1,1];

you don't need the truncation bounds because the parameters (0, 100)
and truncation bounds [-1,1] are both constant and Stan only needs
the (log) probabilty up to a constant term.  You defined the constraints
on ar2 properly and that's all you need.  Same thing with PHIH.

The are other easy wins for vectorization;  you can write this

     for (n in 1:N1){

         MU1[n] ~ normal(0,100);
     }

as

     MU1 ~ normal(0,100);

- Bob

In any case, it is just a state-space model, where the variance of the measurement equation changes over time, and follows a log normal distribution. For example, if we have an AR(1) process in the measurement equation,

Y(t)= alpha*Y(t-1) + exp(h(t)/2)*e(t)

 where e(t) is just white noise. The state equation for the volatilities,

h(t) = muh + phih*(h(t-1) - muh) +eta(t)
eta(t)~N(0,sigma)

and this is really the object of interest...

On Thursday, March 28, 2013 8:50:33 PM UTC-4, Tom Eagle wrote:
> > However, I would like the b's to be correlated, not have a diagonal covariance matrix.  How might I set that up?

If you have a prior covariance matrix, you can just use the syntax in the manual for multi_normal:

coefficients ~ multi_normal(zeros, Sigma);

It is faster to use a precision matrix (the inverse of a covariance matrix), in which case you could do

coefficients ~ multi_normal_prec(zeros, Sigma);

where Sigma is the precision matrix. If you want to use the same covariance matrix or precision matrix for a bunch of coefficient vectors, it can be more efficient to do the multi_normal part manually by incrementing lp__.

Ben

messages.subject: Stochastic Volatility Models
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

I am wondering how STAN deals with a non-linear model like a Stochastic Volatility (SV) one. I attach here a stan file that describes an AR(2) process with SV (and other exogenous regressors), where the error term of the regression is parametrized as in Kim, Sephard and Chib (1998), that is,

exp(h(t)/2)*e(t),e(t)~N(0,1)

The code compiles, and runs. However, I do not know if I am taking a too naive approach here and if the results that I am getting are not proper... SV models are tricky, and usually people (including myself) focus on the approximations derived in Kim et al's paper, or, more recently, using particle filters. Is there any reason why it should not work in STAN? If it works, I think this is a great improvement...

messages.subject_clean: Multivariate normal parameterizations - difficulties with precision/Cholesky
messages.body_plain:
Hi list,

I've been playing around with various ways to sample from a CAR/GMRF, as you may have seen from my posts last month <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/he7BxxHfBfk> trying to replicate the GeoBUGS lip cancer example.

It works with either multi_normal() or lp__ -= with a MVN density (multi_normal.stan.txt and lp_method.stan.txt respectively). Either method gets the same results (which are close but not the same as GeoBUGS). Using lp__ is significantly faster (multi_normal() takes 344s for 2k samples including compilation, lp__ only 35s with compilation).

I'm having trouble getting multi_normal_prec() or multi_normal_cholesky() to work, however.

multi_normal_prec() samples but I get a really poor fit. The random effects are all effectively stuck at 0 and the lp is much worse (826 for the first two models, 2015 for the precision version). Unclear why this is happening. It runs a bit slower than the lp__ method but faster than the regular multi_normal() at 55s.

multi_normal_cholesky() I can't test because I'm unable to run cholesky_decompose() on my covariance matrix. I get an error that it isn't symmetric [Error : error in call to cholesky decomposition; require symmetric matrix, but found; x[0,3]=1.41057e-07:0; x[3,0]=1.41057e-07:0], which I assume may be related to tolerance since the covariance matrix itself is symmetric... (I recognize that the way I have it written out in multi_normal_cholesky.stan.txt negates any speedups from using the cholesky parameterization, but I'm just trying to work backwards from the multi_normal() version to test it out to start).

Any suggestions on what might be happening with the precision or cholesky formulations? I've attached the data/inits and code to run all 4 models (run_models.R.txt).

Also, any thoughts on whether a proper multi_normal_cholesky() implementation would be faster than the lp__ method? It'd certainly look cleaner...

Thanks,
Kyle

Thanks for attaching the code.  The reason the lp__ version is
faster is that it's not checking if the covariance matrix is
positive definite (there are some other checks for finiteness,
but they're fast).

At some point, we'll start evaluating the derivatives
more efficiently inside the probability function compared
to writing out the expression.

We've discussed before whether to keep the error checking
given how expensive it is.  We can probably optimize the code
a bit further.

The Cholesky version should be much faster, either called directly
or implemented directly with lp__.

(Also, I noticed an unused "matrix[N,N] Sigma" delcaration in the lp_method.stan
example.)

> speedups from using the cholesky parameterization, but I'm just trying to work backwards from the multi_normal() version
> to test it out to start).

I didn't understand the parameterization here.
Maybe Ben will.

Absolutely --- this looks like a tolerance issue.
You can always symmetrize explicitly:

for (i in 1:N)
   for (j in (i+1):N)
     Tau[i,j] <- Tau[j,i];

Given that you have:

  Tau <- (tau * tau) * (D - p * A);

and D is clearly diagonal and tau and p are
simple scalars, I don't see how it could not be
exactly symmetric unless A wasn't symmetric coming
in.  So you could probably just symmetrize A if
that's where the issue is.

There are also two things we could do internally to
correct for this.  First, we could increase the error
tolerance -- your inputs look like they're identical to
6 decimal places.  Second, we could use a symmetric
triangular view.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] I am not sure what is going on
messages.body_plain:
Stan internally uses int (32 bit on most platforms)
rather than long (64 bit on most platforms), so even using
it from the command line isn't going to work (though on
Microsoft 64-bit platforms, int might be 64 bit, so
it should work there).

We could change our integer type to long.  We should
probably fix the size across platform one way or the
other.  Not much thought went into making them int other
than long.   I didn't think anyone would use models with
int values above 2 billion.

Something that would work is to convert the integers
to real and then code up whatever distribution you
want directly using lp__.

So instead of

    int<lower=0> y[N];
...
      y[n] ~ poisson(lambda);

use

    real<lower=0> y[N];
...
       lp__ <- lp__ + y[n] * log(lambda) - lgamma(y[n] + 1) - lambda;

This is just the expression for log poisson(y[n]|lambda) using
the fact that lgamma(x+1) = log(x!) if x is an integer.  In fact,
you can just drop the lgamma term because it's a constant (y[n] has
to be data because Stan doesn't support integer params).

This won't be as fast as our vectorized implementation of
Poisson -- you'd have to unfold the vectorizations for that -- but
it should work.

Should we support Poisson with a double variate?

- Bob

Thanks, Bob!

A is indeed symmetric (checked in R via isSymmetric(A) => TRUE), so it must be a tolerance issue.

The Tau code you mention is for the multi_normal_prec() version, which doesn't have problems with symmetry. But I applied the same idea to the cholesky version (attached):

// covariance matrix
    Sigma <- sigma_sq * inverse(D - p * A);

    for (i in 1:N)

        for (j in 1:i)
            Sigma[i,j] <- Sigma[j,i];
    chol_Sigma <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
// CAR model
    beta1 ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, chol_Sigma);

It's rather slow at 285s (as expected, since it's still doing a cholesky decomposition every iteration plus the new loop to force symmetry), but it does get the right fit (i.e. same as the first two models).

So yes, I think allowing for higher tolerances would be useful. But I think I should be able to do the decomposition outside of the model block and thus speed things up significantly. Need to pull out my old matrix algebra book though, as I haven't dealt with that in ages...

messages.subject: Zeroes in Count Model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am using Stan to estimate a binomial count model, y_g ~ binomial(n_g, p_g), for groups defined by demographic characteristics, with a hierarchical model for each group's success probability p_g. Some groups were not sampled from the population, so they have no observed trials and thus no observed successes. Since I want to impute the p_g of these missing groups based on the hierarchical model, I have included them in the data as n_g = 0 and y_g = 0. My intuition is that this is essentially equivalent to treating the empty groups as missing-at-random data, and that they make no contribution to the likelihood. Is this a correct interpretation and a reasonable procedure to follow?

Thanks for your advice!
Devin
